algorithm.title: Routine STI screening in young women

nodes.text: Review sexual history and pregnancy status in women under 25.
Screen annually for chlamydia and gonorrhea by NAAT.
**Chlamydia positive, nonpregnant:** doxycycline and partner treatment.
**Chlamydia positive, pregnant:** azithromycin; test of cure at 4 weeks.
**Gonorrhea positive:** ceftriaxone; cover chlamydia unless excluded.
**New or multiple partners or inconsistent condom use:** add HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B testing.
Offer contraception counseling and condoms; defer cervical cytology until age 21.

nodes.text: Strenuous exertion in heat: heat production exceeds dissipation

nodes.text: Retinal TIA with hemispheric deficits suggests ipsilateral internal carotid atherosclerotic disease.
Obtain carotid duplex ultrasonography to quantify stenosis; obtain urgent brain imaging and ECG.
**Symptomatic 70–99% stenosis with acceptable operative risk:** evaluate CEA within 14 days after neurologic stabilization.
**Symptomatic 50–69% stenosis:** consider selected CEA based on age, sex, and comorbidity.
**Stenosis <50% or complete occlusion:** medical treatment without CEA.
Use antiplatelet and statin therapy; reserve short-course dual antiplatelets for qualifying early high-risk TIA/minor stroke.

Urgent spine surgery consultation for surgical decompression and cervical stabilization
**Surgical candidate with mechanical instability:** surgical decompression plus radiation
**Non-surgical candidate or radio-sensitive tumor:** definitive external beam radiotherapy

fallen frequently becayse of muscle weeks

tenderness over the cervical spine

n-06-q088.boardCall: Rigid peritonitis + pneumoperitoneum (subdiaphragmatic free air) -> emergent exploratory laparotomy.
n-06-q088.hinge: A rigid abdomen with free subdiaphragmatic air confirms perforated viscus and peritonitis, mandating emergent exploratory laparotomy.
n-06-q088.trap: CT scan confirms abdominal pathology, but a patient with peritonitis and obvious free air requires immediate surgery.

A.clue: Fluoroscopic luminal contrast study
A.fit: Not here: contraindicated in suspected perforation, causes severe barium peritonitis

B.clue: Cross-sectional abdominopelvic tomography
B.fit: Not here: free air and rigid peritonitis already established on plain radiograph

C.clue: Gastric acid antisecretory medication
C.fit: Not here: medical suppression ineffective for chemical and bacterial peritonitis

D.clue: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopic visualization
D.fit: Not here: contraindicated, insufflation worsens peritoneal contamination

E.fit: Here: rigid abdomen, absent bowel sounds, subdiaphragmatic free air

nodes.text: Rigid abdomen + free subdiaphragmatic air: perforated viscus
NPO, two large-bore IVs, crystalloids, NG tube
Piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole; IV PPI
Emergent exploratory laparotomy for source control
**Perforated peptic ulcer:** Graham omental patch + H pylori testing
**Hypotension after fluid resuscitation:** norepinephrine; do not delay surgery
**Normal BP, localized tenderness, contained leak on CT:** antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage
Avoid barium and endoscopy when perforation suspected

n-06-q089.boardCall: Lytic bone lesions + hypercalcemia + normocytic anemia + rouleaux on smear -> multiple myeloma.
n-06-q089.hinge: Punched-out lytic bone lesions combined with severe hypercalcemia, anemia, and red cell rouleaux formation indicate multiple myeloma.
n-06-q089.trap: Increased uptake on bone scan tempts metastatic malignancy, but bone scans are cold in pure lytic myeloma.

A.clue: Inactivating CaSR mutation with low urine calcium
A.fit: Not here: lytic bone lesions, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, severe back pain

B.clue: Osteoblastic or osteolytic solid metastases
B.fit: Not here: rouleaux formation on peripheral smear indicates monoclonal paraprotein

C.clue: Monoclonal malignant plasma cell proliferation
C.fit: Here: 67-year-old, lytic bone lesions, calcium 13 mg/dL, rouleaux formation

D.clue: Disorganized bone remodeling
D.fit: Not here: normal calcium typically, no punched-out lytic lesions or rouleaux

E.fit: Not here: punched-out lytic lesions, severe anemia, rouleaux formation

F.fit: Not here: no primary lung/head mass, prominent red cell rouleaux

G.clue: Exogenous retinoid toxicity
G.fit: Not here: lytic skeletal lesions and rouleaux on peripheral smear

H.clue: Granulomatous or excess calcitriol toxicity
H.fit: Not here: punched-out bone destruction, hemoglobin 8 g/dL, rouleaux

nodes.text: Bone pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, rouleaux: evaluate for multiple myeloma
Hypercalcemia: check PTH first
**PTH elevated or high-normal:** primary hyperparathyroidism
**PTH suppressed, PTHrP elevated:** humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (squamous cell)
**PTH suppressed, 25-hydroxyvitamin D elevated:** vitamin D toxicity
**PTH suppressed, M protein or abnormal FLC ratio:** marrow biopsy; ≥ 10% clonal plasma cells confirms
IV saline + zoledronic acid; bortezomib-based triplet induction

n-06-q090.boardCall: Advanced Alzheimer dementia + right lower lobe infiltrate -> aspiration pneumonia due to decreased gag reflex.
n-06-q090.hinge: Impaired swallowing and a depressed protective gag/cough reflex in advanced dementia are the primary predisposing factors for aspiration pneumonia.
n-06-q090.trap: Prior viral illness tempts post-viral infection, but advanced dementia and right base infiltrate point to impaired airway protection.

A.clue: Senescent loss of lung elastic recoil
A.fit: Not here: causes senile emphysema, not dependent aspiration pneumonia

B.clue: Autonomic vascular reflex failure
B.fit: Not here: causes orthostatic hypotension, not lower lobe pneumonia

C.clue: Depressed protective bulbar airway reflexes
C.fit: Here: 87-year-old, Alzheimer dementia, right lung base infiltrate, lethargic

D.clue: Thyroid hormone deficiency
D.fit: Not here: causes hypometabolism and fatigue, not recurrent lobar pneumonia

E.fit: Not here: causes pulmonary venous congestion, not focal right basilar infiltrate

F.fit: Not here: does not impair oropharyngeal coordination or airway defense

G.clue: Cell-mediated immunosenescence
G.fit: Not here: predisposing factor for dependent infiltrate is mechanical aspiration

H.clue: Hypothalamic osmoreceptor blunting
H.fit: Not here: explains dry mucous membranes, but not pneumonia pathogenesis

I.fit: Not here: changes work of breathing, does not cause microaspiration

J.fit: Not here: causes hyponatremic dehydration, not aspiration pneumonia

nodes.text: Dementia + dependent-lobe infiltrate: aspiration pneumonia
Decreased gag reflex and dysphagia impair airway protection
Bedside swallow evaluation or videofluoroscopic study
Standard CAP regimen (ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate)
**Lung abscess or empyema:** anaerobic coverage; drain empyema
Upright meals, diet texture modification
**Recurrent aspiration despite diet modification:** goals-of-care discussion with surrogate

abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.scope: screening recommendations (men 65-75 who smoked), ultrasound imaging, surveillance intervals, elective repair thresholds, rupture
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.core: Older adult with abdominal aortic dilation may remain asymptomatic until expansion or rupture; sudden abdominal/back pain and hypotension require immediate vascular rescue.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking strongest modifiable risk; older age, male sex, family history, hypertension, atherosclerosis
Women have higher rupture risk at smaller diameters; most aneurysms infrarenal
Existing AAA: **diameter and high BP** predict rupture; cholesterol, A1c do not

rows.label: Clues
items: Incidental pulsatile expansile abdominal mass; localized persistent pain suggests symptomatic aneurysm
Rupture triad incompletely present; transient stability may reflect contained retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Blue toe/distal ischemia may result from mural thrombus embolization
Acute back pain unchanged by movement = **referred pain**; prevertebral calcification on x-ray; not disc disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Medial elastin/collagen degradation → progressive enlargement; greater wall radius increases tension

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** diagnoses AAA, generally diameter ≥3 cm; no contrast required
★ Stable suspected rupture or preoperative planning → **CT angiography**
Unstable suspected rupture → bedside ultrasound if immediate; no CT transport delaying surgery
Ultrasound detects aneurysm but cannot reliably exclude rupture; follow symptoms/hemodynamics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Rupture → **urgent vascular repair**, IV access, blood products; avoid delaying for complete workup
Permissive hypotension during transfer/resuscitation until hemorrhage control when clinically feasible
★ Elective repair: **≥5.5 cm men, ≥5.0 cm women**, symptoms; **not if short life expectancy** (metastatic cancer)
Rapid growth ≥0.5 cm/6 months → repair consideration; endovascular versus open based on anatomy/fitness
Smaller asymptomatic lesions → ultrasound surveillance below; refer vascular surgery, manage cardiovascular risks

rows.label: Complications
items: Rupture, thrombosis, distal embolization; repair → AKI, bowel ischemia, endoleak after EVAR
Aortoenteric fistula after prior graft: herald GI bleed → catastrophic hemorrhage; urgent evaluation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **one-time ultrasound men 65–75 who ever smoked**; selectively screen never-smoking men
Women never smoked/no family history → no screening; women smokers/family history → USPSTF evidence insufficient
Smoking cessation, BP control, statin for atherosclerotic disease; lifelong imaging follow-up after EVAR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; shock atypical
Aortic dissection: abrupt chest/back pain, possible pulse deficits or branch ischemia

abdominal-trauma.name: Abdominal trauma
abdominal-trauma.scope: Blunt abdominal trauma (splenic/hepatic laceration, FAST exam, CT scan), penetrating abdominal trauma (stab, gunshot, peritonitis, exploratory laparotomy indications)
abdominal-trauma.core: Abdominal injury after collision, fall, stabbing, or gunshot: hemodynamic status and peritoneal signs determine imaging versus immediate operation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, seat-belt compression, lower rib fractures; anticoagulation increases bleeding risk
Stab wounds may spare viscera; bullets frequently injure multiple structures

rows.label: Clues
items: LUQ pain or referred left shoulder pain → splenic injury; RUQ tenderness → hepatic injury
Distention, ecchymoses, abdominal wall marks; initially benign examination does not exclude bowel injury
★ **Rigidity, rebound, persistent hypotension**, or evisceration → urgent operative assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Solid-organ disruption → intraperitoneal hemorrhage; mesenteric injury → ischemia or delayed perforation
Retroperitoneal injury may produce little intraperitoneal free fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **FAST** at bedside during resuscitation; detects free fluid, not organ-specific injury
★ Stable → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast**; evaluate solid organs, bowel, retroperitoneum
Negative FAST with ongoing shock → search thorax/pelvis, repeat assessment; do not assume safety
Stable anterior stab → local wound exploration or serial examination/CT; trajectory guides evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, large-bore IV access, warmed blood products; massive transfusion for hemorrhagic shock
★ Unstable + positive FAST, peritonitis, or ongoing transfusion need → **exploratory laparotomy**; no CT delay
Stable splenic/hepatic injury → monitored nonoperative care; blush, transient response → angioembolization (older questions: laparotomy)
Enteric contents, uncontrolled bleeding → operation; transperitoneal gunshot → **laparotomy** even if stable; selected stabs observed
Suspected bowel perforation → ceftriaxone + metronidazole, trauma surgery; free subdiaphragmatic air → **laparotomy**, no CT

rows.label: Complications
items: Delayed splenic rupture, abscess, bile leak, abdominal compartment syndrome
Missed hollow-viscus injury → sepsis; splenectomy → overwhelming encapsulated bacterial infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Restraints, airbags, injury-prevention counseling
★ After splenectomy → **pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccines**; fever requires urgent antibiotics

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pelvic hemorrhage: unstable pelvis, negative abdominal FAST
Tension pneumothorax: unilateral absent breath sounds, obstructive shock

abdominal-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established trauma assessment and management principles.

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; distal RTA: urine pH >5.5, hypokalemia; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

acne-vulgaris.name: Acne vulgaris
acne-vulgaris.scope: Comedonal, inflammatory, and nodulocystic acne, topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, oral antibiotics, isotretinoin, photosensitivity counseling
acne-vulgaris.core: Open or closed comedones with variable inflammatory papules, pustules, or nodules reflect pilosebaceous inflammation; severity and scarring determine treatment intensity.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pubertal androgen activity, family history, occlusive products, friction
Exogenous androgens, glucocorticoids, lithium may provoke eruptions; irregular menses/hirsutism suggests androgen excess

rows.label: Clues
items: Face, chest, back commonly involved; mixed lesion types distinguish acne from monomorphic drug eruptions
Deep painful nodules, scars, or substantial psychosocial impairment justify early treatment escalation
Rapid virilization or severe sudden adult onset → assess endocrine/tumor cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: **Androgens (testosterone, DHT) → sebum** + follicular hyperkeratinization + Cutibacterium acnes-driven inflammation
Topical retinoids normalize follicular shedding; benzoyl peroxide is bactericidal without antibiotic resistance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical morphology**; no routine culture or hormone testing for typical adolescent acne
Hyperandrogenic findings → pregnancy test and targeted testosterone/DHEAS evaluation
Before isotretinoin → pregnancy assessment when applicable, baseline lipids and liver enzymes; monitor during treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Combine topical mechanisms** and match intensity below; improvement requires weeks, maintenance prevents relapse
★ **Antibiotics require the topical backbone below**; never antibiotic monotherapy; limit systemic course
Adult hormonally driven acne → combined contraceptive or spironolactone when suitable; avoid spironolactone in pregnancy
★ Isotretinoin → **strict pregnancy prevention/testing**; avoid pregnancy during treatment and 1 month afterward
Pregnancy → azelaic acid/benzoyl peroxide options; avoid retinoids and tetracyclines

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent scars, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, depression; assess suicidal symptoms when present
Doxycycline → esophagitis/photosensitivity; isotretinoin → cheilitis, hypertriglyceridemia, hepatotoxicity
Avoid simultaneous isotretinoin + tetracycline because intracranial hypertension risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Noncomedogenic skin products, sunscreen**, gentle cleansing; avoid picking lesions
Doxycycline: water and remain upright; retinoids: gradual introduction to reduce irritation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Rosacea: flushing/telangiectasia without comedones
Folliculitis: monomorphic follicular pustules, often pruritic
Perioral dermatitis: periorificial papules, vermilion sparing, steroid exposure

acute-bronchitis.name: Acute bronchitis
acute-bronchitis.scope: Viral etiology (influenza, parainfluenza, RSV), persistent postviral cough, absence of pneumonia findings, clinical diagnosis, symptomatic management (NSAIDs, bronchodilators), antibiotic stewardship
acute-bronchitis.core: Acute cough after an upper respiratory illness, with no evidence of pneumonia; usually viral and self-limited.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Influenza, parainfluenza, RSV and other respiratory viruses; close contact during respiratory outbreaks
Smoking and inhaled irritants worsen cough and delay recovery

rows.label: Clues
items: Cough with or without sputum, chest soreness, scattered rhonchi clearing after cough; transient wheezing
Symptoms commonly last 2–3 weeks; postinfectious cough can persist 3–8 weeks
★ **Purulent sputum alone** does not establish bacterial infection
Hypoxemia, focal crackles, sustained fever, tachypnea, hemoptysis → reassess diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient bronchial inflammation, mucus production, and airway hyperresponsiveness after infection
Cough can outlast active viral replication; prolonged symptoms alone do not imply antibiotic benefit

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; routine sputum cultures and chest radiography unnecessary with reassuring vitals and examination
Chest x-ray if focal consolidation, temperature ≥38 °C, HR ≥100/min, or RR ≥24/min
Lower imaging threshold in frail older or immunocompromised adults; pneumonia may lack classic fever
Influenza/COVID testing if result changes antivirals or isolation; paroxysms/exposure → pertussis PCR

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **No antibiotics** for uncomplicated disease regardless of cough duration
Hydration, acetaminophen or ibuprofen for discomfort; dextromethorphan may offer limited cough relief
★ **Albuterol only with wheezing/airflow obstruction**; systemic steroids not routine
High-risk suspected influenza → oseltamivir; suspected pertussis → azithromycin to limit transmission

rows.label: Complications
items: Sleep disruption, chest wall strain, transient bronchospasm; persistent cough requires review for another cause
Unnecessary antibiotics → C. difficile, adverse reactions, antimicrobial resistance

rows.label: Prevention
items: Respiratory hygiene, smoking cessation, influenza/COVID vaccination; set expectations for cough duration
Return for worsening dyspnea, recurrent fever, dehydration, or new focal symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pneumonia: infiltrate and systemic illness or focal consolidation
Asthma: recurrent episodic cough/wheeze, reversible obstruction
Pertussis: prolonged paroxysms, posttussive emesis, exposure history

acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, cirrhosis, low-output heart failure (prerenal despite overload); baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment (dipstick blood, few RBCs), prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → tubulointerstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**
Anuria despite patent catheter after pelvic surgery + hydronephrosis → ureteral injury/ligation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia (postoperative oliguria, high urine specific gravity) → saline bolus; congestion → loop diuretic; no reflex fluids in overload
Stop nephrotoxins, all NSAIDs including celecoxib (intra-articular steroid for joint pain); persistent AIN → glucocorticoids; renal-dose drugs
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function
Contrast in high-risk CKD → **periprocedural IV isotonic saline**; diuretics, mannitol, metformin stop don't protect
ACR now limits contrast prophylaxis mainly to eGFR <30; older exam questions may expect wider hydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

acute-otitis-media.name: Acute otitis media
acute-otitis-media.scope: Bulging erythematous tympanic membrane, impaired mobility, oral amoxicillin first-line, amoxicillin-clavulanate, tympanostomy indications
acute-otitis-media.core: Acute otalgia with middle-ear effusion and a bulging tympanic membrane identifies acute otitis media; age, laterality, and severity guide antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young age, daycare, viral URI, tobacco smoke exposure, absent breastfeeding
Craniofacial abnormalities and eustachian tube dysfunction increase recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: Ear tugging, fever, irritability, poor feeding; spontaneous perforation causes new otorrhea
★ **Postauricular swelling/tenderness, protruding pinna** → mastoiditis
Erythematous membrane alone, especially during crying, insufficient for diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: URI-related eustachian edema traps fluid; pneumococcus, nontypeable H influenzae, Moraxella commonly infect middle ear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pneumatic otoscopy**: reduced mobility supports effusion; moderate/severe bulging or nonexternal otorrhea diagnostic
Mild bulging requires recent otalgia or intense erythema; no effusion → no AOM diagnosis
Tympanometry if effusion uncertain; no routine imaging/cultures; suspected mastoiditis → **contrast CT temporal bones/head**
Failure after 48–72 h → repeat examination; persistent effusion alone does not mean antibiotic failure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Acetaminophen or ibuprofen** for pain regardless of antibiotic decision
★ When treating → **amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day**; 10 days if <2 years or severe
Recent amoxicillin within 30 days, purulent conjunctivitis, or amoxicillin failure → amoxicillin-clavulanate
Selected older nonsevere cases → 5–7 days; severe illness/complication or oral intolerance changes regimen
★ Recurrent AOM **≥3/6 months or ≥4/12 months** → tube evaluation; effusion required at candidacy assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Conductive hearing loss, membrane perforation, mastoiditis, rare intracranial infection
Effusion ≥3 months → hearing assessment; tubes considered for bilateral persistent fluid with hearing difficulty

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pneumococcal/influenza vaccination, breastfeeding, smoke avoidance; no routine prophylactic antibiotics
Observe speech/hearing development in recurrent disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Otitis media with effusion: fluid, retracted gray membrane, no acute inflammation → **observe, no antibiotics**
Otitis externa: canal inflammation, pain with tragus/pinna movement
Referred dental/TMJ pain: normal middle-ear examination

acute-respiratory-failure.name: Acute respiratory failure
acute-respiratory-failure.scope: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (type 1), hypercapnic respiratory failure (type 2), noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP), indications for invasive mechanical ventilation
acute-respiratory-failure.core: Acute inability to maintain oxygenation or ventilation demands simultaneous cause treatment and escalating respiratory support, guided by work of breathing and airway safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS, PE → oxygenation failure
COPD, neuromuscular weakness, obesity hypoventilation, sedatives → ventilation failure; overlap common

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, hypoxemia, diaphoresis; hypercapnia may cause headache, somnolence, asterixis
★ **Exhaustion, declining consciousness, silent chest, paradoxical breathing** → impending respiratory arrest
Normal saturation on supplemental oxygen does not exclude dangerous CO₂ retention

rows.label: Pathophys
items: V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment lowers PaO₂; shunt may resist oxygen alone
Inadequate alveolar ventilation raises PaCO₂; abrupt rise causes respiratory acidosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry + ABG** when severe distress, hypercapnia concern, or escalating support
Chest radiograph, ECG, bedside lung/cardiac ultrasound; infection/PE testing follows clinical context
Trend pH, gases, respiratory rate, mentation and effort; do not wait for an extreme number
Chronic compensated hypercapnia has elevated bicarbonate; pH decline identifies acute deterioration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oxygen immediately**, treat cause; target SpO₂ 88–92% with CO₂-retention risk, usually 92–96% otherwise
Hypoxemic failure needing more than conventional oxygen → high-flow nasal cannula, close reassessment
★ Awake cooperative COPD + respiratory acidosis → **BiPAP**; cardiogenic edema → CPAP/BiPAP plus diuresis/nitrates
★ **Intubate** for airway failure, refractory hypoxemia, shock, arrest, exhaustion, or worsening despite noninvasive support
Avoid NIV with vomiting, unprotected airway, copious secretions, major facial trauma; reassess within 1–2 h

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrhythmia, multiorgan failure; delayed intubation worsens outcome
Positive pressure → hypotension/barotrauma; invasive ventilation → pneumonia and ventilator-induced lung injury
Ventilated ARDS: low tidal volume using predicted body weight, limited plateau pressure; prone if severe

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, respiratory vaccination, disease control, cautious sedatives, aspiration precautions
High-risk extubation patients may benefit from planned NIV rather than rescue after deterioration
Awake, stable, low ventilator support → **spontaneous breathing trial** to wean, before tracheostomy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metabolic acidosis: compensatory tachypnea with low CO₂
Panic hyperventilation: respiratory alkalosis without sustained gas-exchange failure

table.title: Gas-exchange classification; room air when feasible

adjustment-disorder.name: Adjustment disorder
adjustment-disorder.scope: Identifiable psychosocial stressor within 3 months, marked distress or functional impairment, resolution within 6 months, psychotherapy
adjustment-disorder.core: Disproportionate distress or functional impairment beginning within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, without meeting criteria for another disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Relationship loss, illness, job loss, relocation, school difficulty; limited social support or coping resources
Prior psychiatric illness, ongoing adversity, cumulative stress; assess cultural context and expected responses

rows.label: Clues
items: Anxiety, depressed mood, mixed emotions, or conduct disturbance linked temporally to the event
★ Symptoms resolve within **6 months after stressor/consequences end**; may persist with ongoing stress
Sleep difficulty, worry, withdrawal, reduced performance; impairment exceeds an expected adaptive response

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stress-related maladaptive coping and emotional dysregulation; no required traumatic exposure or unique biomarker

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical chronology** plus functional assessment; clarify symptoms before and after the stressor
★ Screen **suicidality**, substance use, mania, psychosis; investigate medical causes suggested by history
Full major-depressive syndrome takes precedence even when triggered by a clear life event
Reassess persistence, escalating severity, or loss of temporal connection; diagnosis may change over time

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Brief psychotherapy**, problem solving, CBT, coping skills; strengthen support and reduce modifiable stress
Address sleep routines, daily structure, school/work accommodations and practical resources
Medication usually unnecessary; severe acute anxiety/insomnia → brief **benzodiazepine** (older exams); SSRIs take weeks
Suicidal intent, inability to maintain safety, or severe deterioration → urgent psychiatric assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Self-harm, suicide risk, substance misuse, occupational or academic decline
Persistent symptoms may evolve into major depression, anxiety disorder, or another defined condition

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early transition support, coping skills, follow-up until recovery; involve trusted supports with consent

rows.label: Mimics
items: Major depression: ≥2 weeks, ≥5 symptoms including depressed mood/anhedonia
PTSD/acute stress disorder: qualifying trauma plus intrusion/avoidance; PTSD >1 month, acute stress 3 days–1 month
Normal grief: fluctuating loss-focused sadness with preserved self-worth and adaptive function
GAD: ≥6 months of multi-domain worry, not tied to one recent stressor

adjustment-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR teaching.

adolescent-preventive-care.name: Adolescent preventive care
adolescent-preventive-care.scope: Leading causes of death, injury prevention, HEADSS psychosocial screening, adolescent screening tests
adolescent-preventive-care.core: Private, developmentally appropriate preventive visits identify injury risk, mental illness, substance use, sexual health needs, and barriers to healthy development.

rows.label: Who
items: All adolescents annually; explain confidentiality and safety exceptions, with some time alone
Leading death cause: **unintentional injury**, then suicide, homicide; risk varies by age and population

rows.label: Start/stop
items: HEADSS: Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression; include strengths and safety
★ Annual **depression and suicide-risk screening from 12**; assess younger patients when concerned
HIV once during adolescence, repeat with ongoing risk; lipids once at 17–21 years

rows.label: Test
items: ★ BP, BMI, development; **chlamydia/gonorrhea annually** for sexually active females <25
Exposure-site STI testing for MSM; syphilis/TB/anemia testing by risk
Assess sleep, nutrition, eating disorders, substances/vaping, violence, school, sexual coercion

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Positive suicide screen → **brief safety assessment**, urgent evaluation for imminent risk
Post-menarche → pregnancy/STI prevention, contraception; treat STIs; substance-use counseling; accessible follow-up
Counsel seat belts, helmets, no impaired/distracted driving; secure firearms unloaded and locked

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **No routine Pap before 21**, even with sexual activity; STI screening uses separate tests
Depression screening alone misses some suicide risk; ask directly about thoughts and plans
Early post-menarche: irregular cycles normal, no hormone testing; update HPV, MenACWY, Tdap

adrenal-insufficiency.name: Adrenal insufficiency
adrenal-insufficiency.scope: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), secondary adrenal insufficiency, cosyntropin stimulation test, morning serum cortisol, hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement, adrenal crisis
adrenal-insufficiency.core: Weight loss, fatigue, orthostasis, and hyponatremia, or unexplained pressor-resistant shock after illness or interruption of glucocorticoids.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: autoimmune destruction, TB, bilateral hemorrhage, metastases; associated autoimmune thyroid disease
★ Secondary: **prolonged glucocorticoids**, pituitary disease/surgery/apoplexy; abrupt withdrawal risks crisis
Crisis triggers: infection, trauma, surgery, missed replacement, vomiting

rows.label: Clues
items: Anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, weakness; hypoglycemia, eosinophilia
Crisis: fever, confusion, severe volume depletion; symptoms may worsen rapidly during intercurrent illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortisol deficiency reduces vascular catecholamine response and increases ADH
Primary gland failure removes mineralocorticoids; secondary disease retains renin–angiotensin-driven aldosterone

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **8 AM cortisol + ACTH**; very low cortisol supports, clearly high values argue against insufficiency
★ Equivocal basal cortisol → **cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation**; inadequate assay-specific peak confirms impaired reserve
Traditional stimulated cutoff ≈18 µg/dL; newer assays may use ≈14–15; interpret laboratory standard
Primary → 21-hydroxylase antibodies, selected adrenal CT; secondary → pituitary evaluation/MRI
Recent pituitary injury may initially show normal cosyntropin response; clinical suspicion still matters

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crisis → draw blood if feasible, **IV hydrocortisone + isotonic saline**, dextrose for hypoglycemia
Do not wait for confirmatory results; treat precipitant and correct electrolytes carefully
Coexisting hypothyroidism → glucocorticoid replacement before levothyroxine to avoid decompensation

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated crisis → arrhythmia, circulatory collapse, death; chronic undertreatment → impaired function
Excess replacement → osteoporosis, diabetes, Cushingoid features

rows.label: Prevention
items: Stress-dose plan, emergency injectable hydrocortisone, medical alert ID; taper prolonged systemic steroids
Vomiting prevents absorption → parenteral replacement and urgent evaluation; teach sick-day plans to caregivers

rows.label: Mimics
items: SIADH: euvolemia, normal potassium and cortisol reserve
Sepsis: infection may coexist and trigger crisis
Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, cold intolerance, weight gain

table.title: Primary versus secondary
rows: Low/inappropriately normal ACTH; potassium usually normal

adrenal-insufficiency.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching; cortisol cutoffs are assay dependent.

adrenal-masses.name: Adrenal masses
adrenal-masses.scope: Adrenal incidentaloma, adrenocortical carcinoma, functional vs nonfunctional evaluation, pheochromocytoma, hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, hyperandrogenism (DHEA-S), adrenal CT imaging, adrenalectomy indications
adrenal-masses.core: An incidental adrenal lesion requires two decisions: malignant potential on imaging and clinically important hormone secretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incidental detection increases with age; known extra-adrenal cancer raises metastatic risk
MEN2/VHL/NF1 predispose to pheochromocytoma; most incidental lesions are benign cortical adenomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic; weight loss, flank pain, rapid growth, or mixed steroid excess suggest carcinoma
Episodic headache/palpitations/diaphoresis → catecholamines; proximal weakness/easy bruising → cortisol excess
Resistant hypertension/hypokalemia → aldosterone; rapid virilization → adrenal androgen secretion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortical tumors may secrete cortisol, aldosterone, or androgens; medullary tumors secrete catecholamines
Autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH and contralateral adrenal function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast adrenal CT** first; assess density, homogeneity, size, invasion; indeterminate → dedicated imaging
★ **1 mg overnight dexamethasone**: cortisol >1.8 µg/dL suggests autonomy; confirm ACTH independence
Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines if lesion not clearly benign or pheochromocytoma symptoms
Hypertension/hypokalemia → aldosterone/renin; virilization/possible carcinoma → DHEA-S, precursors; **high DHEA-S** → adrenal source
★ **Never biopsy before excluding pheochromocytoma**; biopsy rarely distinguishes adenoma from cortical carcinoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinically significant unilateral hormone excess → **adrenalectomy**; suspected carcinoma requires preoperative staging
Pheochromocytoma: **phenoxybenzamine** alpha blockade, volume repletion before surgery; beta blockade only after alpha
Mild cortisol autonomy: individualize surgery by diabetes, hypertension, skeletal disease, and operative risk
Indeterminate unoperated lesion → repeat CT/MRI in 6–12 months; growth prompts reassessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Pheochromocytoma manipulation → hypertensive crisis; carcinoma → metastases
Postoperative adrenal insufficiency after cortisol-producing tumor removal → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Address cortisol-associated cardiometabolic and bone risk; genetic counseling for syndromic catecholamine tumors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Myelolipoma: macroscopic fat on CT
Adrenal metastasis: cancer history, often bilateral; biopsy only if management changes
Adrenal hemorrhage: acute pain, anticoagulation/trauma context, evolving imaging appearance

table.title: Imaging changes the answer
rows: Benign; no further imaging regardless of size

adult-immunizations.name: Adult immunizations
adult-immunizations.scope: Routine adult vaccines, immunocompromised and HIV, pregnancy, live-vaccine contraindications, chronic medical conditions (COPD, diabetes, liver disease), vaccine counseling and addressing hesitancy
adult-immunizations.core: Match vaccination to age, prior doses, pregnancy, immune status, and exposure risk; missed series resume without restarting.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **HepB**: all 19–59; ≥60 with risk/request; health worker anti-HBs negative post-series → revaccinate
**HIV any CD4**, liver disease/alcohol, COPD, diabetes, smoking → pneumococcal <50; liver → HepA/HepB
Asplenia → pneumococcal, MenACWY, MenB, Hib; HIV → MenACWY

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Pregnancy: **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 wk**; inactivated influenza any trimester
Maternal RSV: Abrysvo at 32–36 wk, September–January; previous pregnancy dose → infant antibody instead
RSV once: all ≥75; ages 50–74 with increased severe-disease risk

rows.label: Test
items: Anti-HBs/anti-HAV/VZV IgG positive → immune, skip; otherwise **do not delay vaccination** for serology
★ Immunocompromised ≥19 → recombinant zoster; HIV CD4 ≥200 permits MMR/varicella if nonimmune
HPV started <15 → two doses; ≥15 or immunocompromised → three

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **No live MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza**: severe immunosuppression, pregnancy (nonimmune → postpartum)
PCV15 → PPSV23: ≥8 weeks immunocompromised; older exams: PPSV23 alone; mild illness/antibiotics: no deferral
Hesitancy → elicit concern; inactivated influenza cannot cause flu, coincidental virus; refusal → document, revisit

table.title: Routine adult schedule
rows: Annual influenza; updated COVID-19 for all adults
Tdap once, then either every 10 years
PCV20/21 alone; PCV15 → PPSV23 after 1 year

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**
Hospital day 2–5 or postoperative: new agitation, hallucinations, autonomic signs → suspect **unreported alcohol use**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; dexmedetomidine adjunct; **chlorpromazine**/antipsychotics lower seizure threshold, prolong QT

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine
Pregnancy: seizures, adrenergic surge → fetal hypoxia; **maternal withdrawal** is greatest immediate fetal risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure
Anticholinergic delirium: dry skin, urinary retention; diaphoresis favors withdrawal

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common
rows: Visual/auditory/tactile hallucinations; clear sensorium; vitals near normal
Disorientation, hallucinations, fever, tremor, marked autonomic instability

alpha-1-antitrypsin-deficiency.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
alpha-1-antitrypsin-deficiency.scope: SERPINA1 gene mutation (PiZZ phenotype), panacinar basilar emphysema in young nonsmokers, liver cirrhosis/hepatoma, PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules, serum AAT level and phenotype
alpha-1-antitrypsin-deficiency.core: Premature obstructive lung disease with unexplained liver disease or a family history suggests inherited alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal codominant **SERPINA1** variants; PiZZ phenotype causes severe deficiency
Smoking, secondhand smoke, occupational dust and fumes accelerate pulmonary injury

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Young nonsmoker with **basilar panacinar emphysema**, exertional dyspnea, and persistent airflow obstruction
Neonatal cholestasis or adult hepatic dysfunction; liver and lung disease may occur independently
Hyperinflation, diminished breath sounds; advanced disease → hypoxemia and right-heart strain

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Deficient circulating antiprotease → unopposed neutrophil elastase and alveolar wall destruction
Misfolded protein retained in hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum → cellular injury, fibrosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Serum AAT level** → phenotype or genotype confirmation; acute inflammation can falsely elevate levels
Test all adults with COPD, unexplained bronchiectasis, or unexplained chronic liver disease
Spirometry establishes obstruction; chest CT defines distribution; LFTs and ultrasound assess hepatic injury
★ Liver biopsy, if obtained: **PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules**; not required for routine diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Smoking cessation** plus inhaled bronchodilators; pulmonary rehabilitation and oxygen for qualifying chronic hypoxemia
IV AAT augmentation for selected nonsmokers with severe deficiency and established emphysema; specialist selection
Augmentation does not treat liver injury; decompensated cirrhosis → liver transplantation
End-stage pulmonary disease despite treatment → lung transplantation evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, recurrent respiratory infections
Cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; hepatic cancer surveillance once cirrhosis develops

rows.label: Prevention
items: Offer genetic counseling and testing to first-degree relatives; genotype rather than level alone
Influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal vaccines; hepatitis A/B vaccination with liver disease
Avoid excess alcohol and hepatotoxic exposures; monitor pulmonary function and liver tests

rows.label: Mimics
items: Smoking-related emphysema: predominantly upper-lobe centriacinar destruction
Cystic fibrosis: bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, elevated sweat chloride
Other cirrhosis: viral, alcohol, metabolic causes without the characteristic inherited pulmonary pattern

alpha-1-antitrypsin-deficiency.evidence: Not checked online; established AAT deficiency diagnosis and management.

amenorrhea.name: Amenorrhea
amenorrhea.scope: Primary amenorrhea (Turner syndrome, Mullerian agenesis, AIS), secondary amenorrhea (pregnancy, functional hypothalamic, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid, premature ovarian insufficiency, Asherman), diagnostic algorithm
amenorrhea.core: Absent menses requires pregnancy exclusion, then assessment of anatomy, estrogen status, thyroid function, prolactin, and the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Weight loss, intense exercise, psychosocial stress; pituitary disease, dopamine-blocking drugs, thyroid dysfunction
Uterine instrumentation, chemotherapy, autoimmune disease; congenital reproductive tract or chromosomal abnormalities

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary: no menarche by 15; absent breast development by 13 also warrants evaluation
Secondary: ≥3 months absent previously regular cycles, or ≥6 months previously irregular
Galactorrhea/headache, visual symptoms, hot flashes, hirsutism, cyclic pelvic pain guide localization
Galactorrhea, hypothyroid signs → TSH first (TRH raises prolactin); unexplained prolactin → pituitary MRI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Amenorrhea results from axis suppression, ovarian failure, chronic anovulation, or absent/obstructed outflow
Functional: energy deficit disrupts pulsatile GnRH → irregular, low gonadotropins, low estrogen

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **hCG first**, even if unlikely or premenarchal (ovulation precedes menarche); ultrasound assesses uterus, ovaries
★ TSH, prolactin, **FSH/estradiol**; low estradiol: high FSH → ovarian failure; low/normal FSH → hypothalamic/pituitary
**Progestin challenge**: bleed → anovulation (estrogen, outflow intact); no bleed → low estrogen/outflow defect, check FSH
POI before 40: ≥4 months irregular/absent cycles with FSH >25 IU/L; repeat if uncertain
Post-instrumentation amenorrhea with otherwise normal endocrine testing → saline sonography/hysteroscopy for adhesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Functional hypothalamic → **restore energy intake**, reduce excessive exercise, address eating disorder/stress
Prolactinoma → cabergoline; thyroid disease → correct thyroid function; Asherman → hysteroscopic adhesiolysis
★ POI → **estrogen replacement plus progestogen if uterus present**, usually until natural menopause age
Chronic anovulation → endometrial protection with cyclic progestogen or combined contraception; treat underlying cause
Hematocolpos → **transvaginal incision, drainage**; imperforate hymen → **cruciate hymenotomy**; ultrasound if anatomy unclear

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoestrogenism → infertility, low bone density; prolonged unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia
Absent uterus differs from absent ovaries: fertility options depend on anatomy and gonadal function

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate nutrition, avoid overtraining/uterine injury; intermittent ovulation still requires contraception

rows.label: Mimics
items: Imperforate hymen: cyclic pain, bulging bluish hymen, hematocolpos
PCOS: hyperandrogenism with chronic anovulation, estrogen generally preserved

table.title: Primary amenorrhea: high FSH or absent uterus → karyotype

anorectal-disorders.name: Anorectal disorders
anorectal-disorders.scope: Anal fissure, internal and external hemorrhoids, anorectal abscess, fistula-in-ano, pruritus ani, topical vasodilators, fiber, sitz baths
anorectal-disorders.core: Anal pain, bleeding, swelling, or drainage requires inspection and focused examination; pain pattern distinguishes fissure, thrombosis, and infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constipation, straining, pregnancy, prolonged sitting; Crohn disease, diabetes, immunosuppression increase infection risk
Irritant soaps, moisture, fecal seepage contribute to pruritus ani

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Pain out of proportion, fever, spreading erythema, crepitus** → evaluate necrotizing perineal infection urgently
Posterior midline fissure common; lateral/multiple fissures suggest Crohn disease, infection, or malignancy
Internal hemorrhoids lie above dentate line; prolapse may require manual reduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fissure causes internal sphincter spasm and local ischemia; hemorrhoids represent enlarged vascular cushions
Cryptoglandular infection creates abscess; persistent epithelialized tract can become a fistula

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Inspection first**, gentle DRE/anoscopy when tolerable; do not force painful fissure examination
Deep pain without visible lesion → CT/MRI for occult abscess; recurrent fistula → pelvic MRI
Rectal bleeding with anemia, weight loss, bowel change, or screening indication → colon evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Fiber, fluids, stool softening, **sitz baths**; fissure → topical anesthetic, nitroglycerin or diltiazem
Refractory chronic fissure → botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy after continence-risk assessment
Internal hemorrhoids persisting despite conservative measures → rubber-band ligation; advanced prolapse → surgery
★ Abscess → **incision and drainage**; antibiotics added for cellulitis, systemic illness, or immunosuppression
Fistula → colorectal surgery; painful thrombosed external hemorrhoid within 72 hours → consider excision

rows.label: Complications
items: Abscess recurrence, fistula, sepsis; sphincter injury → fecal incontinence
Chronic bleeding → iron deficiency; pruritus → excoriations and secondary infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid straining and prolonged toilet sitting; gentle cleansing, dry skin, barrier ointment for seepage

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anal cancer: persistent irregular ulcer/mass or large wart-like lesion, biopsy required
Proctitis: urgency, tenesmus, mucous discharge
Pinworm: nocturnal itch, especially children; tape test

table.title: Local patterns
rows: Tearing defecation pain; bright blood on paper
Recurrent purulent drainage from external opening

anorectal-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established colorectal teaching.

antepartum-fetal-surveillance.name: Antepartum fetal surveillance
antepartum-fetal-surveillance.scope: Nonstress test (reactive vs nonreactive), biophysical profile (BPP components and scoring), modified BPP, contraction stress test, umbilical artery Doppler, indications (FGR, diabetes, post-term, decreased movement)
antepartum-fetal-surveillance.core: Assess fetal well-being when stillbirth risk is elevated; abnormal screening generally needs confirmation or delivery according to gestation and severity.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ FGR, high-risk diabetes, hypertension, post-term pregnancy, decreased fetal movement

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Often around 32 weeks; earlier if severe risk and delivery would be considered
Decreased movement → prompt NST/fluid assessment; ongoing frequency based on underlying disorder

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Reactive NST ≥32 weeks: **two 15-beat accelerations lasting 15 seconds**, within 20 minutes
Before 32 weeks use 10 × 10; extend observation to 40 minutes for sleep
★ **BPP**: NST plus four ultrasound components; each 0 or 2, maximum 10

rows.label: IF positive
items: Nonreactive NST → stimulation/extended tracing, then BPP or selected contraction stress test
★ BPP ≤4 generally → delivery; 6 → repeat within 24 hours or term delivery
Low fluid requires evaluation despite score; umbilical Doppler guides FGR decisions

rows.label: Traps
items: BPP 8–10 reassuring only with normal fluid; modified BPP = NST + fluid assessment
CST: late decelerations with ≥50% contractions positive; avoid when labor contraindicated
False positives common; reassuring test does not predict acute abruption or cord accident

table.title: Ultrasound BPP: normal criteria during 30-minute observation

antepartum-fetal-surveillance.evidence: Indications checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG surveillance guidance](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2021/06/indications-for-outpatient-antenatal-fetal-surveillance); interpretation established obstetric teaching.

anticoagulants.name: Anticoagulants
anticoagulants.scope: Warfarin (CYP interactions, INR monitoring, reversal with vitamin K and PCC), heparin and LMWH (protamine reversal, HIT), direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, reversal agents)
anticoagulants.core: Anticoagulants prevent clot extension and embolization; drug choice depends on indication, renal function, pregnancy, and bleeding risk.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ **DOACs**: most nonvalvular AF and VTE; warfarin: mechanical valves, rheumatic mitral stenosis
LMWH: pregnancy; UFH: rapid reversibility or severe renal impairment

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling → ↓II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S
UFH/LMWH enhance antithrombin; UFH inhibits IIa/Xa, LMWH predominantly Xa
Apixaban/rivaroxaban directly inhibit Xa; dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin

rows.label: Adverse
items: Bleeding with all; warfarin → early skin necrosis, fetal injury
★ **HIT**: platelet fall >50%, usually days 5–10; thrombosis more characteristic than bleeding
High INR + bowel obstruction, hemoglobin drop → **intramural small-bowel hematoma**

rows.label: Avoid
items: Suspected HIT → stop every heparin source; start argatroban or another nonheparin anticoagulant
Warfarin initiation during acute HIT; DOACs for mechanical valves or high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome

rows.label: Interactions
items: Warfarin ↑: amiodarone, TMP-SMX/metronidazole, **fluoroquinolones**; ↓: rifampin, vitamin K-rich diet
DOAC exposure altered by strong P-glycoprotein/CYP3A modifiers; NSAIDs/antiplatelets increase bleeding

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Warfarin **INR**, usually 2–3; UFH aPTT/anti-Xa; LMWH/DOACs: renal function, CBC
No routine INR titration for DOACs; LMWH anti-Xa only selected situations

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Acute VTE warfarin → overlap parenteral anticoagulant ≥5 days and until therapeutic INR
Historical Xa antidote andexanet: US sales ended December 2025; use local PCC-based reversal protocols

atopic-dermatitis.name: Atopic dermatitis
atopic-dermatitis.scope: Atopic dermatitis, pruritus, flexural lichenification, emollients and topical corticosteroids, complications (eczema herpeticum, bacterial infection)
atopic-dermatitis.core: Chronic relapsing itchy eczema with xerosis; infants often have facial/extensor disease, while older children develop flexural lichenification.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Personal/family atopy, impaired skin barrier, dry climate; soaps, wool, fragrances, heat can trigger flares
Asthma and allergic rhinitis commonly coexist; scratching and bacterial colonization exacerbate inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Excoriations, erythema, oozing during flares; sleep disturbance and chronic thickening from rubbing
★ **Painful monomorphic punched-out erosions**, fever, rapid spread → eczema herpeticum
Honey-colored crusts, pustules, warmth or spreading erythema → secondary bacterial infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Barrier dysfunction increases water loss and allergen penetration; type 2 inflammation drives itch–scratch cycle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** by itch, distribution, chronicity; no routine serum IgE/food allergy panels
Atypical/refractory disease → assess contact allergy, infestation, immune deficiency; selected patch testing
Suspected HSV complication → lesion PCR, but begin treatment before results if clinically convincing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **thick emollient**, short lukewarm bathing, fragrance-free cleanser; apply moisturizer promptly afterward
★ Flares → **topical corticosteroid**, potency by site/severity: triamcinolone on body; hydrocortisone on face/folds
Tacrolimus/pimecrolimus for sensitive sites or steroid-sparing maintenance; wet wraps for selected severe flares
Refractory moderate/severe disease → phototherapy or dupilumab; avoid chronic systemic glucocorticoids
★ Eczema herpeticum → **systemic acyclovir** now; ocular involvement → ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: S aureus superinfection, disseminated HSV, sleep loss, psychosocial burden
Excess topical steroid potency/duration → skin atrophy, striae; dupilumab → conjunctivitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrier care, trigger reduction, short nails; intermittent maintenance anti-inflammatory treatment at recurrent sites
No empiric elimination diets without confirmed clinical allergy; avoid routine antibiotics for uninfected eczema

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contact dermatitis: exposure-shaped distribution, patch-test association
Scabies: nocturnal household itch, burrows in webs/wrists
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy scale, less itching

benign-breast-conditions.name: Benign breast conditions
benign-breast-conditions.scope: Fibroadenoma, fibrocystic changes, intraductal papilloma, breast cyst, fat necrosis, galactocele, breast abscess
benign-breast-conditions.core: Breast symptoms require age-directed imaging and clinical–radiologic concordance; a benign-appearing examination alone cannot exclude malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive hormonal cycling; milk stasis; breast trauma or prior surgery
Smoking predisposes to recurrent subareolar abscess
**Cracked, excoriated nipples** → main portal of entry for lactational mastitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Galactocele: cystic lactational/postlactational mass, no inflammation, varies with feeds; fat–fluid level on imaging
Mastitis: focal tender erythema, fever, no fluctuance; abscess adds **fluctuance**; often Staphylococcus aureus
★ Spontaneous unilateral **bloody single-duct discharge** → usually **papilloma**; exclude malignancy, persistent → surgical evaluation
Nonbloody discharge only on expression, normal exam → **physiologic**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormone-responsive stromal/glandular tissue produces cyclic changes; duct obstruction causes retained secretions
Adipose injury causes inflammatory necrosis and calcification that can resemble cancer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Palpable mass **<30 years → ultrasound**; ≥30 → diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound
Suspicious solid lesion or imaging–exam discordance → **core needle biopsy**
Simple cyst: anechoic, thin-walled, posterior enhancement; no solid component
Nonlactational abscess or persistent inflammation after antibiotics → exclude underlying carcinoma
Cyclic bilateral nodularity, no dominant mass → **reexamine after menses**, before imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Painful simple cyst → aspiration; nonbloody fluid + full collapse → benign; bloody fluid/residual mass → **biopsy**
Fibroadenoma → observe when concordant; excise if rapidly enlarging, large or symptomatic
Breast pain, no mass, young, normal exam → **reassurance**; fibrocystic pain → supportive bra, topical/oral NSAID
★ Mastitis → **dicloxacillin/cephalexin**, keep breastfeeding/pumping; abscess → add needle/incision drainage; MRSA → clindamycin
Tender lactating lump, no erythema/fever → **warm compresses**, keep nursing; persistent galactocele → aspiration

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent periductal abscess → fistula; incomplete drainage → persistent infection
Proliferative lesions with atypia increase future cancer risk; simple cysts do not

rows.label: Prevention
items: Effective breast emptying during lactation; smoking cessation for recurrent periductal disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cancer: irregular fixed mass, retraction or suspicious nodes
Phyllodes: rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial mass requiring excision

table.title: Common benign findings
rows: Early postpartum; bilateral tense tender breasts, low fever

benign-breast-conditions.evidence: Not checked online; established breast diagnostic principles.

benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.scope: Lower urinary tract symptoms, medical therapy, urinary retention and obstructive uropathy
benign-prostatic-hyperplasia.core: Aging man with hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, and nocturia from benign periurethral prostatic enlargement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, androgen exposure, family history, obesity/metabolic syndrome
Anticholinergics, opioids, and sympathomimetic decongestants can precipitate retention

rows.label: Clues
items: Storage symptoms: urgency, frequency; voiding symptoms: straining, intermittency, terminal dribbling
Smooth, symmetric enlarged prostate; size correlates imperfectly with symptom severity
★ **Painful inability to void** with palpable bladder → acute urinary retention
Renal dysfunction or bilateral hydronephrosis suggests high-pressure obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dihydrotestosterone-driven transition-zone hyperplasia + alpha-adrenergic smooth-muscle tone obstruct bladder outlet

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**, symptom score, examination; review medications and neurologic disease
Postvoid residual if incomplete emptying suspected; creatinine/renal ultrasound for obstruction or renal impairment
PSA after shared decision-making if result changes management; elevation not specific for cancer

rows.label: Tx
items: Mild, nonbothersome → observation; reduce evening fluids, caffeine, alcohol; timed voiding
★ Acute retention → **urethral catheter**, then alpha-blocker and voiding trial; suprapubic drainage if catheterization fails
★ Refractory symptoms, retention, recurrent UTIs, stones, renal impairment → **TURP or other outlet procedure**
Monitor urine output/electrolytes after relief of prolonged obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Overflow incontinence, recurrent infection, bladder stones, postrenal AKI
Postobstructive diuresis; surgery → bleeding, retrograde ejaculation, urethral stricture

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid precipitating drugs; reassess progressive symptoms and residual volume
BPH does not transform into prostate cancer; continue independent cancer-risk discussion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Prostate cancer: hard asymmetric nodule
Prostatitis: tender prostate, fever; neurogenic bladder: neurologic disease, altered bladder sensation

table.title: Medication selection
rows: Large gland; reduce progression over months

brain-abscess.name: Brain abscess
brain-abscess.scope: Direct spread (otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis), hematogenous spread (endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease), ring-enhancing lesion, polymicrobial, aspiration, empiric antibiotics
brain-abscess.core: Headache with a focal deficit or seizure and an enhancing intracranial mass after infection should prompt urgent abscess evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe or cerebellum; sinusitis/dental infection → frontal lobe
Endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease, pulmonary infection → hematogenous seeding, often multiple lesions
Neurosurgery/penetrating trauma → staphylococci; immunosuppression → fungi, Nocardia, Toxoplasma

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever may be absent; nausea, papilledema or deteriorating consciousness suggest increased ICP
★ **Ring enhancement with central diffusion restriction** strongly favors pyogenic abscess

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal cerebritis progresses to encapsulated pus with surrounding vasogenic edema
Contiguous infections often polymicrobial: streptococci and anaerobes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI with DWI** preferred; contrast CT if MRI unavailable
Blood cultures before antibiotics; aspirated material → aerobic/anaerobic cultures and targeted molecular testing
★ **Avoid LP**: low diagnostic yield, mass-effect herniation risk
Search source: ENT/dental assessment; echocardiography for bacteremia, multiple lesions, or endocarditis signs

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Ceftriaxone + metronidazole**; add vancomycin for trauma, neurosurgery, or staphylococcal concern
Urgent neurosurgical aspiration/drainage for sizable accessible lesions, mass effect, or diagnostic uncertainty
Small stable lesions may receive antibiotics with serial MRI; usual IV course 6–8 weeks
Stable, aspiration within 24 hours → cultures first may be reasonable; never delay antibiotics if deteriorating
Dexamethasone only for severe edema/impending herniation; levetiracetam for seizures

rows.label: Complications
items: Intraventricular rupture, ventriculitis, herniation, persistent focal deficits, epilepsy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat contiguous infection and endocarditis; correct infectious source and relevant cardiac lesions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Necrotic tumor: central diffusion restriction less typical, no infectious source
Toxoplasmosis: advanced HIV, multiple basal ganglia lesions
Neurocysticercosis: cyst with scolex, exposure in endemic region

cardiomyopathies.name: Cardiomyopathies
cardiomyopathies.scope: Dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, restrictive cardiomyopathy, stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, viral myocarditis, diagnostic evaluation, management
cardiomyopathies.core: Myocardial disease causes pump failure, impaired filling, dynamic obstruction, or arrhythmias; echocardiography defines the phenotype.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dilated: familial disease, alcohol, anthracyclines, peripartum state, **viral myocarditis**
Hypertrophic: autosomal dominant sarcomeric variants; restrictive: amyloid, hemochromatosis, radiation
Takotsubo: emotional/physical stress; myocarditis: recent viral illness, immune checkpoint inhibitors

rows.label: Clues
items: Exertional dyspnea, edema, elevated JVP; **displaced PMI**, S3 → dilated LV; syncope/ventricular arrhythmia signals danger
★ Obstructive HCM murmur **↑Valsalva/standing**, ↓squatting/handgrip; exertional presyncope
Myocarditis: chest discomfort, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, acute heart failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sarcomere dysfunction or myocardial injury → remodeling; infiltration → reduced ventricular compliance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG, troponin, BNP → transthoracic echo**; assess coronary ischemia when suspected
Cardiac MRI: inflammation, scar, infiltrative patterns; iron studies or monoclonal protein testing when relevant
Endomyocardial biopsy: selected fulminant unexplained failure, malignant arrhythmias, suspected giant-cell myocarditis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ HFrEF: **ARNI, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor**; loop diuretic for congestion
Obstructive HCM: nonvasodilating beta-blocker (propranolol, metoprolol); alternative verapamil/diltiazem
Refractory obstruction → myosin inhibitor, disopyramide, or septal reduction; avoid dehydration and vasodilators
Restrictive disease: cautious diuresis, treat cause; Takotsubo: supportive care after excluding ACS
Myocarditis with shock → ICU, circulatory support; no routine antiviral or immunosuppression

rows.label: Complications
items: Sudden cardiac death, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism; advanced failure → transplantation evaluation
★ HCM with cardiac arrest or major sudden-death risk → **ICD** consideration

rows.label: Prevention
items: Screen first-degree relatives in inherited disease; avoid cardiotoxins
Myocarditis: restrict strenuous exercise until clinical recovery and reassessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ischemic cardiomyopathy: obstructive coronary disease explains dysfunction
Constrictive pericarditis: pericardial disease, respiratory ventricular interdependence
Aortic stenosis: murmur softer with standing/Valsalva, unlike obstructive HCM

table.title: Echo phenotype
rows: Enlarged ventricles, diffuse hypokinesia, reduced EF
Transient apical ballooning beyond coronary territory

cardiomyopathies.evidence: HCM checked 2026-10-30: [AHA/ACC 2024](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/05/06/15/12/2024-hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy-gl); other content established teaching.

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax** (painless curtain-like monocular vision loss), contralateral weakness, aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion
Retinal **Hollenhorst plaque** (cholesterol embolus) → ulcerated ipsilateral carotid plaque

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Hyperperfusion after revascularization → headache, seizures, brain hemorrhage; driven by **postoperative hypertension**
New deficit after endarterectomy → **noncontrast head CT** first: hemorrhage vs carotid thrombosis; no heparin/tPA beforehand
★ Expanding neck hematoma with stridor → **open wound/emergent neck exploration**; no imaging delay

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms
Giant cell arteritis: headache, jaw claudication, ↑ESR; vision loss often persistent

table.title: Symptomatic ipsilateral stenosis
rows: Selected patients: age, sex, comorbidity matter

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.scope: Median nerve entrapment, pregnancy and endocrine risk factors, Phalen and Tinel tests, wrist splinting, corticosteroid injection, surgical release
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.core: Median nerve compression at the wrist causes nocturnal paresthesias in the thumb, index, middle, and radial ring fingers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pregnancy/fluid retention, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis
Forceful repetitive hand activity, wrist trauma; dialysis-associated amyloid in selected patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Shaking hand relieves symptoms; driving or sustained wrist flexion aggravates symptoms
★ **Thenar weakness/atrophy**, dropping objects, impaired thumb opposition → advanced nerve injury
Central palm sensation usually spared because palmar cutaneous branch bypasses tunnel
Bilateral symptoms common; isolated little-finger symptoms argue against median neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Raised pressure beneath transverse carpal ligament → median nerve ischemia/demyelination
Long-standing compression progresses to axonal loss and persistent motor impairment

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical history + **Phalen/Tinel or carpal compression** findings support clinical diagnosis
Phalen: sustained wrist flexion; Tinel: percussion over median nerve reproduces distal paresthesia
★ **Nerve-conduction studies/EMG** for atypical presentation, severity assessment, or uncertain diagnosis before surgery
Targeted TSH/glucose testing when systemic disease suspected; routine wrist imaging unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Mild/moderate or **pregnancy** → **neutral-position night wrist splint**, ergonomics; pregnancy often resolves postpartum
Local corticosteroid injection for persistent symptoms or short-term relief
★ Severe deficit, denervation, or failed conservative care → **surgical carpal tunnel release**
NSAIDs do not relieve the underlying compression; avoid repeated ineffective analgesic-only management

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent sensory loss and thenar wasting if severe compression persists
Injection → transient hyperglycemia, rare nerve injury; surgery → scar pain or incomplete release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce prolonged wrist flexion/extension and forceful vibration; adjust workstation and tools
Manage contributing endocrine/inflammatory disease; reassess worsening motor function promptly

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical radiculopathy: neck pain, dermatomal weakness/reflex changes
Ulnar neuropathy: little finger/ulnar ring symptoms, interosseous weakness
Pronator syndrome: proximal forearm pain with palmar sensory involvement

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.name: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.scope: Central line infection, organisms, line removal, prevention
catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.core: Fever or rigors in a patient with an intravascular catheter, especially during infusion, raises concern for catheter-related bacteremia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long catheter dwell time, femoral placement, parenteral nutrition, immunosuppression, hemodialysis
Poor asepsis, frequent hub manipulation; tunneled devices and ports also susceptible

rows.label: Clues
items: Exit-site erythema or drainage may occur; normal insertion-site appearance does not exclude infection
★ **Hypotension, persistent bacteremia**, new murmur, or embolic signs → complicated infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Skin flora migrate externally or contaminated hubs seed intraluminal biofilm
Biofilm limits antibiotic penetration; S aureus and Candida frequently seed distant sites

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Before antibiotics: **paired peripheral and catheter blood cultures**, labelled by source
Same organism with catheter culture positive ≥2 h earlier supports catheter source
Culture removed catheter tip when infection suspected; no routine tip culture after elective removal
Repeat blood cultures to document clearance; persistent positivity → endocarditis, infected thrombus, abscess evaluation
S aureus bacteremia → echocardiography, TEE when high risk; assess metastatic foci

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric **IV vancomycin** (MRSA, coagulase-negative staph); sepsis/neutropenia → add cefepime; adjust to cultures
★ **Remove line** for shock, tunnel infection, endocarditis, persistent bacteremia, S aureus, Pseudomonas, or fungi
Candida → echinocandin; MSSA → cefazolin or nafcillin; enterococcal treatment follows susceptibilities
Selected stable long-term line infections with coagulase-negative staphylococci → systemic antibiotics + antibiotic lock
Uncomplicated S aureus bacteremia: ≥14 days after clearance; endocarditis/deep infection usually requires 4–6 weeks

rows.label: Complications
items: Endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, osteomyelitis, septic emboli, shock
Unnecessary device retention → relapse; repeated placement → thrombosis and vascular injury
Suppurative thrombophlebitis: fluctuant, purulent vein after line removal → **surgical vein excision**, not compresses

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Hand hygiene, chlorhexidine skin preparation, maximal sterile barrier** during insertion
Scrub hubs, sterile dressings, daily necessity review, prompt removal of unnecessary lines
Avoid routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics or scheduled catheter replacement solely to prevent infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contaminated blood culture: single skin-flora isolate without corroborating cultures or illness
Infusate reaction: temporal symptoms without reproducible bacteremia
Catheter thrombosis: swelling, poor flow; cultures negative unless infected
Wound/abdominal source: local findings; benign exam + gram-positive bacteremia → catheter

table.title: Organism pattern
rows: S epidermidis: leading biofilm/port-pocket infection; distinguish contamination
Parenteral nutrition, broad antibiotics; remove catheter
