Avoid barium studies or diagnostic endoscopy when perforation suspected; water-soluble contrast only for selected questions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, large-bore IVs, isotonic crystalloid**, analgesia; immediate surgical consultation
★ Prompt **piperacillin-tazobactam** or ceftriaxone + metronidazole; cover enteric gram-negatives/anaerobes
Nasogastric decompression for upper GI leak/ileus; IV proton-pump inhibitor for ulcer perforation
Urgent operative repair/resection and washout for free perforation; norepinephrine if shock persists after fluids
Selected stable contained leak may receive antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage with close surgical observation

rows.label: Complications
items: Intra-abdominal abscess, septic shock, multiorgan failure, fistula; anastomotic leak after repair

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H. pylori after ulcer disease; avoid unnecessary NSAIDs, use gastroprotection when ulcer risk high
Treat causal disease, optimize postoperative leak recognition; reassess persistent fever/pain after procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pancreatitis: elevated lipase, characteristic epigastric/back pain without typical pneumoperitoneum
Mesenteric ischemia: initially pain out of proportion; later peritonitis indicates necrosis/perforation
Postoperative free air: may be expected, but instability/peritonitis demands leak evaluation

gastrointestinal-perforation.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency general surgery and sepsis source-control teaching.

gestational-trophoblastic-disease.name: Gestational trophoblastic disease
gestational-trophoblastic-disease.scope: Complete hydatidiform mole, partial hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, suction curettage, serial beta-hCG surveillance, contraception
gestational-trophoblastic-disease.core: Abnormal trophoblastic proliferation causes excessive hCG, bleeding, and vesicular placental tissue; persistent hCG after evacuation suggests gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior molar pregnancy, extremes of reproductive age; choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Vaginal bleeding, hyperemesis, uterus larger than dates, bilateral theca lutein cysts
★ **Preeclampsia before 20 weeks** or gestational thyrotoxicosis → suspect mole
Postpregnancy bleeding with cough/hemoptysis or neurologic symptoms → metastatic trophoblastic malignancy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal fertilization produces proliferative hydropic villi; high hCG stimulates thyroid and ovarian receptors
Choriocarcinoma lacks chorionic villi and spreads hematogenously, especially to lungs, vagina, brain

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Quantitative **β-hCG + pelvic ultrasound**; snowstorm/multicystic placental appearance may be absent early
Evacuated tissue histopathology confirms; p57 absent in complete mole, retained in partial mole
★ Postevacuation **hCG plateau over 3 weeks or rise over 2 weeks** → evaluate GTN
Suspected neoplasia → chest imaging and stage/risk assessment; avoid biopsy of vascular vaginal metastasis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stabilize bleeding → **suction curettage**; send tissue; give anti-D if Rh-negative
Hysterectomy an option when fertility not desired; surveillance remains necessary
Low-risk GTN → methotrexate or actinomycin D; high-risk → multiagent chemotherapy
hCG every 1–2 weeks until normal; partial: reconfirm after 1 month; complete: monthly for 6 months

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, thyroid storm, early hypertensive disease, invasive mole, metastatic malignancy
Chemotherapy toxicity; prognosis often excellent even with metastatic disease when treated

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reliable contraception during hCG surveillance; combined OCPs acceptable; defer pregnancy until follow-up complete
Future pregnancy → early ultrasound and postpregnancy hCG assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Multiple gestation: high hCG with recognizable normally developing fetuses
Missed abortion: nonviable gestation without trophoblastic overgrowth

table.title: Molar subtypes
rows: Usually triploid; maternal + two paternal sets

gestational-trophoblastic-disease.evidence: Surveillance checked 2026-10-30: [FIGO 2025 update](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12411817/); remaining pathology established teaching.

giant-cell-arteritis.name: Giant cell arteritis
giant-cell-arteritis.scope: Giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, vision loss
giant-cell-arteritis.core: New headache with jaw claudication or visual symptoms after age 50 requires immediate glucocorticoids to prevent irreversible blindness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, female sex, Northern European ancestry; frequently overlaps polymyalgia rheumatica
Age <50 makes this diagnosis very unlikely

rows.label: Clues
items: Scalp tenderness, abnormal temporal artery, fever, weight loss, fatigue
★ **Transient monocular loss, diplopia, or sudden painless visual loss** → ocular ischemia
PMR: bilateral shoulder/hip aching, morning stiffness >45 minutes; true muscle strength preserved

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Granulomatous inflammation of large/medium arteries → intimal proliferation and ischemic narrowing
Posterior ciliary artery involvement causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ESR/CRP and CBC**: inflammation, thrombocytosis, normocytic anemia support; normal markers do not fully exclude
★ **Temporal artery biopsy** confirms; skip lesions can cause false negative, so obtain adequate segment
Ultrasound halo sign useful in experienced centers; arrange testing promptly after treatment begins
Assess pulses, arm pressures, bruits; CTA/MRA for suspected aortic/branch-vessel involvement
PMR: elevated inflammatory markers, normal CK; screen all PMR patients for cranial/visual symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected cranial GCA → **high-dose oral prednisone now**, before biopsy
★ Threatened or established visual loss → **IV methylprednisolone** urgently; ophthalmology consultation
Taper slowly with symptom/marker monitoring; tocilizumab can reduce steroid exposure in selected patients
Isolated PMR → lower-dose prednisone, no biopsy unless cranial/visual symptoms; no prompt improvement → reconsider diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent blindness, often sequential fellow-eye involvement; stroke, aortic aneurysm/dissection
Prolonged steroids → infection, diabetes, cataracts, osteoporosis; IL-6 blockade can suppress inflammatory markers

rows.label: Prevention
items: Bone protection and fracture-risk assessment during prolonged steroids; monitor BP/glucose
Educate about recurrent visual symptoms, jaw pain, limb claudication; evaluate aorta over time

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy: vascular risks, no systemic inflammatory syndrome
Myositis: objective proximal weakness, elevated CK
TMJ disease: local joint pain/clicking rather than chewing-induced ischemic fatigue

giant-cell-arteritis.evidence: Not checked online; established rheumatologic emergency and PMR management.

glycogen-storage-diseases.name: Glycogen storage diseases
glycogen-storage-diseases.scope: Von Gierke disease (type I), Pompe disease (type II), Cori disease (type III), McArdle disease (type V), exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria, fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly
glycogen-storage-diseases.core: Inherited glycogen disorders separate into fasting-intolerant hepatic disease, exercise-intolerant skeletal muscle disease, and infantile cardiomyopathy with hypotonia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually autosomal recessive; consanguinity or affected siblings; presentation from infancy to adulthood

rows.label: Clues
items: Hepatic forms: hepatomegaly and fasting intolerance; hypoglycemic seizures possible
★ **Second-wind phenomenon** after brief rest or reduced intensity suggests muscle phosphorylase deficiency
★ Floppy infant with **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**, macroglossia and respiratory weakness → urgent metabolic evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective glycogen synthesis/breakdown impairs glucose release or muscle energy supply
Lysosomal glycogen accumulation uniquely produces the multisystem storage phenotype in type II

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, lactate, lipids, uric acid, CK**, liver enzymes; correlate abnormalities with phenotype
Enzyme assay and molecular testing confirm subtype; echocardiography when cardiac involvement possible
Suspected muscle glycogenosis: exercise-associated CK/myoglobin elevation; nonischemic forearm testing may support diagnosis
Avoid diagnostic prolonged fasting in infants or severe hypoglycemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Hepatic forms: **frequent feeds/uncooked cornstarch**; acute hypoglycemia or no enteral intake → IV dextrose
Type I: restrict fructose/galactose; monitor metabolic control and renal/hepatic disease
Type III: high-protein diet plus fasting avoidance; individualized cornstarch
Type II: **alglucosidase alfa** enzyme replacement promptly; ventilatory/cardiac support
Type V: graded aerobic conditioning, avoid intense isometric exertion; simple carbohydrate before planned exercise

rows.label: Complications
items: Type I: hepatic adenomas, CKD, gout; type III: fibrosis and cardiomyopathy
Muscle forms: rhabdomyolysis, AKI; untreated infantile type II: cardiorespiratory failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Genetic counseling; sick-day feeding plans and avoidance of prolonged fasting in hepatic disease
Educate muscle-disease patients to stop exertion for cramps/dark urine and maintain hydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Fatty-acid oxidation defects: fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia, abnormal acylcarnitines
Muscular dystrophy: progressive weakness rather than episodic metabolic exercise intolerance

table.title: Enzyme and pattern
rows: Exercise cramps/myoglobinuria; flat exercise lactate rise

glycogen-storage-diseases.evidence: Not checked online; established metabolic phenotypes and foundational management.

gout.name: Gout and crystal arthropathy
gout.scope: Acute gout, chronic gout and urate lowering, pseudogout (CPPD)
gout.core: Abrupt intensely painful inflammatory arthritis from crystal deposition; gout and CPPD require different long-term prevention despite similar flare management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gout: CKD, obesity, alcohol, purines/fructose, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin
CPPD: older age, joint injury, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia
Flares follow surgery, dehydration, illness, or changes in urate concentration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid-onset red swollen tender joint, often overnight; fever possible
Chronic gout: tophi on ears/olecranon, erosive arthritis; recurrent flares separated by asymptomatic intervals
CPPD in younger adults → investigate associated metabolic disorders

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Crystal phagocytosis activates inflammasome/IL-1 → neutrophilic synovitis
Most hyperuricemia reflects reduced renal urate excretion rather than excessive production

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First/atypical acute monoarthritis → **arthrocentesis**, polarized microscopy, Gram stain/culture
★ **Crystals do not exclude septic arthritis**; serum urate may be normal during gout flare
Chronic imaging: punched-out defects with overhanging edges; ultrasound double-contour sign supports urate deposition

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute crystal flare → **indomethacin/other NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid**; joint steroid after excluding infection
NSAID failure → switch class; older exam questions may expect potent NSAID, e.g. indomethacin
CKD/ulcer/anticoagulation → favor steroid; adjust colchicine for renal impairment/interactions; avoid NSAIDs in advanced CKD
★ Urate lowering: **allopurinol first-line**, including CKD; start low, titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL
Urate lowering doesn't treat flares; continue through flares; may start mid-flare (older exam questions: wait)

rows.label: Complications
items: Gout: destructive arthritis, uric-acid stones; CPPD: chronic degenerative/inflammatory arthropathy
Allopurinol hypersensitivity; colchicine → diarrhea/neuromyopathy
Xanthine-oxidase inhibitors + azathioprine/6-MP → severe marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Urate lowering: **tophi, joint damage, ≥2 flares/year**; first flare with CKD ≥3/stones/urate >9 → consider
Starting urate lowering → colchicine/NSAID prophylaxis 3–6 months; serial urate monitoring; not for isolated hyperuricemia
Uncomplicated first flare → **limit alcohol/fructose**, lose weight; thiazide → losartan; keep indicated aspirin
Before allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01 testing with Southeast Asian/African American ancestry; CPPD lacks crystal-depleting drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: positive culture, bacteremia risk; aspiration essential when uncertain
Cellulitis: superficial inflammation, less restriction of passive joint motion
RA: persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis

gout.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACR gout guideline 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10563586/), [ACR gout education 2025](https://rheumatology.org/patients/gout); CPPD established teaching.

guillain-barre-syndrome.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
guillain-barre-syndrome.scope: Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni), albuminocytologic dissociation, IVIG or plasma exchange
guillain-barre-syndrome.core: Rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with reduced reflexes after infection suggests immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy; respiratory and autonomic monitoring are immediate priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Campylobacter gastroenteritis, respiratory viral infection, CMV; typically 1–3 weeks earlier
Rare postvaccination association; infection poses greater risk than routine vaccination

rows.label: Clues
items: Leg weakness ascends over days, paresthesias, back/radicular pain, bilateral facial weakness
★ **Areflexia with flaccid weakness**; sensory complaints usually exceed objective sensory loss
★ **BP swings, arrhythmias, urinary retention**, bulbar dysfunction indicate severe disease
Miller Fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; maximal weakness usually within 4 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Molecular mimicry triggers antibodies against peripheral nerve components
Demyelinating conduction block most common in US; axonal variants also occur

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serial **forced vital capacity and inspiratory force**; pulse oximetry misses early ventilatory weakness
LP: **↑protein with few cells**; CSF may be normal during first week
Nerve conduction studies: slowing/conduction block or axonal loss; normal early studies do not exclude
Marked CSF pleocytosis, sensory level, or early sphincter dysfunction → reconsider mimics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Admit for telemetry, swallowing evaluation, frequent strength and breathing assessments
Declining FVC, often <20 mL/kg, weak cough/bulbar dysfunction → **early elective intubation**
★ **IVIG or plasma exchange** for nonambulatory, rapidly progressive, or significant respiratory/bulbar disease
Do not combine routinely; **glucocorticoids do not help**
DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, nutrition, pain control, PT; avoid succinylcholine because hyperkalemia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, aspiration, lethal dysautonomia, VTE, pressure injuries
Residual weakness, neuropathic pain, prolonged fatigue; recovery usually spans months

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prophylaxis; early rehabilitation and immobilization precautions reduce secondary injury
Monitor for treatment-related fluctuations; progression beyond 8 weeks raises concern for CIDP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Transverse myelitis: sensory level, early bladder dysfunction, eventual hyperreflexia
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness, normal reflexes and sensation
Botulism: descending paralysis, pupillary dysfunction, preserved sensorium

guillain-barre-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established neurology teaching.

heat-related-illness.name: Heat-related illness
heat-related-illness.scope: Heat exhaustion, classic and exertional heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia and NMS contrast
heat-related-illness.core: Heat exposure with neurologic dysfunction signals heat stroke, requiring immediate cooling before laboratory confirmation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Classic: older adults (**impaired thirst**), heat waves, impaired sweating, anticholinergics, limited water access
Exertional: strenuous activity, poor acclimatization, heavy equipment, stimulant use

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Delirium, seizures, or coma** distinguish heat stroke from uncomplicated heat exhaustion
Tachycardia, hypotension, vomiting; sweating may persist despite severe heat injury
Core temperature often >40 °C; lower readings after cooling do not exclude heat stroke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heat production exceeds dissipation → endothelial injury, systemic inflammation, cellular dysfunction
Sweat losses → hypovolemia; excessive free water intake can produce hyponatremia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Rectal temperature**; oral, axillary, and tympanic measurements may underestimate severity
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis, liver enzymes, coagulation studies; repeat for evolving injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, remove clothing, **rapid whole-body cooling**; do not delay for transport or tests
Exertional: cold-water immersion, else evaporative cooling; classic: evaporative; no alcohol sponging; stop active cooling near 39 °C
★ **IV isotonic crystalloid** for hypovolemia; benzodiazepines for seizures or shivering
Avoid antipyretics; environmental hyperthermia has no elevated hypothalamic temperature set point

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, ARDS, persistent neurologic deficits
Delayed liver injury despite initial clinical improvement

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Gradual acclimatization**, scheduled rest, shade, hydration, cooling access
Avoid strenuous exercise during peak heat; monitor vulnerable adults during heat waves

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sepsis: infectious focus, fever unrelated to environmental load
Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic exposure, clonus, hyperreflexia

heat-related-illness.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency medicine teaching.

huntington-disease.name: Huntington disease
huntington-disease.scope: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, anticipation, chorea, caudate and putamen atrophy, psychiatric manifestations
huntington-disease.core: An inherited progressive movement, cognitive, and psychiatric disorder often emerges in midlife, with earlier onset across successive generations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Autosomal dominant HTT CAG expansion**; each child of an affected heterozygote has 50% risk
Paternal transmission particularly associated with repeat expansion and anticipation

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular flowing chorea, motor impersistence, impaired voluntary saccades; later rigidity and bradykinesia
Irritability, depression, impulsivity, psychosis; executive dysfunction progresses to dementia
Psychiatric symptoms may precede movement disorder; juvenile disease often rigid with seizures
★ **Suicidal ideation** requires direct safety assessment, especially around diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Toxic huntingtin damages striatal GABAergic neurons; reduced indirect-pathway inhibition increases unwanted movement
Caudate/putamen atrophy produces enlarged frontal horns on brain imaging

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Compatible phenotype/family history → **HTT genetic testing** after informed counseling
≥40 repeats: full penetrance; 36–39: reduced penetrance; intermediate alleles can expand in offspring
MRI supports differential diagnosis; gene testing confirms, imaging alone does not
Predictive testing of asymptomatic adults → consent, psychological assessment and genetic counseling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling chorea → **tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine**; monitor depression, suicidality and parkinsonism
Antipsychotics such as risperidone for psychosis/aggression; SSRIs for depression/anxiety
Physical/occupational and speech-swallow support; nutrition, fall prevention and advance-care planning
No established cure; avoid dopamine-depleting agents in active suicidality or inadequately treated depression

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, falls, weight loss, loss of independence; suicide
VMAT2 inhibitors → sedation, akathisia, depression; antipsychotics → metabolic and motor adverse effects

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reproductive counseling, prenatal/preimplantation testing options; defer predictive testing of asymptomatic minors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Wilson disease: younger onset, liver disease, low ceruloplasmin; potentially treatable
Tardive dyskinesia: dopamine-blocker exposure, predominant orobuccolingual stereotypies

huntington-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

hypercalcemia.name: Hypercalcemia
hypercalcemia.scope: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, milk-alkali syndrome, IV saline resuscitation, calcitonin, bisphosphonates
hypercalcemia.core: Elevated calcium causes stones, constipation, polyuria, weakness, and neuropsychiatric changes; PTH distinguishes hormone-driven disease from other causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia, malignancy, prolonged immobilization
Thiazides, lithium, excess vitamin D or calcium/absorbable alkali, granulomatous disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Dehydration, nausea, abdominal pain, reduced reflexes; ECG may show shortened QT
★ **Calcium >14 mg/dL**, confusion, arrhythmia, or severe volume depletion → urgent treatment
Primary hyperparathyroidism often asymptomatic; malignancy-associated disease tends to progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PTH promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention while increasing phosphate excretion
Hypercalcemia impairs renal concentration → dehydration, reduced calcium clearance, self-reinforcing elevation
High filtered calcium exceeds tubular reabsorption → **hypercalciuria** → calcium stones

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm with repeat total/albumin-adjusted or **ionized calcium**, especially with altered proteins or critical illness
★ **Intact PTH first**; elevated or inappropriately normal → PTH-dependent
Suppressed PTH → PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, malignancy/myeloma evaluation guided by context
Primary disease versus FHH → urine calcium; clearance ratio <0.01 favors FHH, with overlap
Parathyroid imaging localizes before surgery; never establishes biochemical diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe/symptomatic → **IV isotonic saline**, then calcitonin for rapid temporary lowering
★ **Denosumab** (favored, esp renal limitation/refractory) or **IV zoledronic acid/pamidronate** for sustained malignancy control
Calcitriol-mediated disease → glucocorticoids; dialysis for refractory life-threatening elevation or inability to hydrate
Primary disease: surgery for symptoms, age <50, calcium >1 above ULN, osteoporosis/fracture, stones, eGFR <60
Stop causative supplements/drugs; loop diuretic only for fluid overload, not routine calcium elimination

rows.label: Complications
items: Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, AKI, osteoporosis/fractures, pancreatitis
Calcitonin tachyphylaxis after 48–72 hours; antiresorptives can cause hypocalcemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration, avoid excess calcium/alkali; monitor calcium, renal function, and bone density when observing primary disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: FHH: lifelong mild elevation, family history, hypocalciuria; surgery ineffective
Pseudohypercalcemia: high protein-bound calcium but normal ionized fraction

hypercalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established calcium evaluation and emergency management.

hyperemesis-gravidarum.name: Hyperemesis gravidarum
hyperemesis-gravidarum.scope: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, ketonuria, electrolyte abnormalities, Wernicke encephalopathy, dietary modifications, antiemetics, IV hydration
hyperemesis-gravidarum.core: Severe early-pregnancy nausea and vomiting with inability to eat/drink normally, impaired functioning, and often dehydration or weight loss.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Previous hyperemesis, multiple gestation, molar pregnancy, family history; begins usually before 16 weeks

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthostasis, tachycardia, reduced urine, weight loss often >5% prepregnancy weight
Hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; starvation may produce ketosis/acidosis
★ Confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia → **Wernicke encephalopathy**; triad may be incomplete
Mild transaminitis or transient low TSH can occur; fever/focal abdominal pain suggests another diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental hormonal signals, including GDF15, drive nausea; prolonged starvation depletes thiamine and electrolytes
Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis reflects hCG stimulation rather than intrinsic thyroid autoimmunity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical assessment of intake, weight and hydration; electrolytes, renal function, urinalysis, liver tests
Ultrasound assesses gestational dating, multiplicity, or suspected trophoblastic disease
★ **Ketonuria not required, not a severity marker**; older exam questions may expect urine ketones for starvation/dehydration
Thyroid testing for severe/atypical cases; goiter or ophthalmopathy suggests Graves rather than pregnancy physiology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Mild nausea: small frequent meals, avoid triggers; **pyridoxine + doxylamine** first-line
Persistent vomiting → promethazine, metoclopramide, or ondansetron; combine agents from different classes if needed
★ Dehydration/electrolytes, PO intolerance → **admit: IV saline + potassium**, parenteral antiemetics; replace low magnesium
Prolonged vomiting → thiamine before dextrose; suspected Wernicke → high-dose IV thiamine immediately
Refractory disease → enteral nutrition preferred; corticosteroids after other options fail

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, malnutrition, esophageal injury, venous thrombosis; severe electrolyte abnormalities → arrhythmia
Refeeding syndrome during nutritional recovery; monitor phosphorus, magnesium, potassium
Nonsevere disease, mild weight loss → no significant fetal harm; severe disease → low birth weight

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early antiemetics in recurrent disease; maintain hydration/nutrition; hospitalized patients need VTE-risk assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: diarrhea, infectious contacts, short nonpregnancy-linked course
DKA: hyperglycemia or euglycemic pregnancy ketoacidosis with high anion gap
Appendicitis: focal progressive tenderness and inflammatory signs

hyperemesis-gravidarum.evidence: Ketones/thiamine checked 2026-10-30: [RCOG Green-top 69, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1111/1471-0528.17739); remaining content established teaching.

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul (deep) breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema (Cushing triad), hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia

table.title: Biochemistry; ketones and HCO₃ in mmol/L

hypertensive-crises.name: Hypertensive crises
hypertensive-crises.scope: Hypertensive urgency, hypertensive emergency, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside
hypertensive-crises.core: Severe BP elevation becomes an emergency when new target-organ injury accompanies it; the number alone does not determine urgency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antihypertensives, CKD, sympathomimetics; clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy, renovascular disease, catecholamine excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Usually **>180/120 mm Hg** with AKI, ACS, pulmonary edema, stroke, or dissection
Encephalopathy: headache, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance; papilledema or retinal hemorrhages

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoregulatory failure → endothelial injury, microangiopathy, tissue ischemia; cerebral vasogenic edema in PRES

rows.label: Dx
items: Repeat correctly sized cuff reading; examine neurologic status, fundi, pulses, heart and lungs
Creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, ECG; troponin with cardiac symptoms
Neurologic symptoms → head CT; suspected dissection → CTA chest/aorta
MRI posterior vasogenic edema supports PRES after hemorrhage exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most emergencies: ICU, titratable IV **nicardipine, labetalol, or nitroprusside**
★ Reduce MAP ≤25% first hour → approximately 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours; then gradual normalization
★ No acute injury: treat pain/anxiety, restart or adjust oral drugs, arrange close outpatient follow-up
Avoid rapid IV lowering for asymptomatic BP; avoid immediate-release nifedipine
Nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use or renal/hepatic dysfunction; monitor closely

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral hemorrhage, renal failure, MI; overly rapid lowering → cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication access and adherence; home BP monitoring; avoid cocaine and amphetamines

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pain/anxiety elevation: improves after trigger control, no acute injury
Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension thresholds differ; avoid applying generic reduction targets

hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.name: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.scope: infantile presentation (nonbilious projectile vomiting, olive mass), hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, ultrasound diagnosis, fluid resuscitation, pyloromyotomy
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.core: A hungry young infant with progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting suggests gastric outlet obstruction from pyloric muscle hypertrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually 2–8 weeks old; more common in firstborn boys and with family history
Early-life macrolide exposure, especially erythromycin; bottle feeding and maternal smoking associated

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting becomes forceful after feeds; dehydration, weight loss, fewer wet diapers
★ **Palpable epigastric/right-upper-quadrant olive**, visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis
★ **Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis** after prolonged vomiting; labs may initially be normal
Bilious emesis is atypical and demands urgent evaluation for obstruction distal to ampulla

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypertrophied pyloric circular muscle obstructs gastric emptying without blocking bile drainage into distal bowel
Gastric HCl loss and contraction activate aldosterone → renal potassium loss; severe depletion causes paradoxical aciduria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ultrasound first**: thickened elongated pylorus with impaired passage
Typical thresholds: muscle thickness ≥3 mm, channel length ≥15 mm; interpret by infant size
Equivocal early study → repeat ultrasound; upper GI series can show string sign if uncertainty persists
Electrolytes, glucose, renal function, blood gas assess resuscitation needs before anesthesia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO + IV isotonic saline**, glucose-containing maintenance fluid; correct chloride deficit first
Replace potassium after confirming urine output; monitor hydration and electrolytes
★ **Pyloromyotomy after normalization** of volume and alkalosis; medical stabilization precedes definitive surgery
NG decompression when ongoing vomiting/distention; postoperative feeds advanced with surgical team

rows.label: Complications
items: Severe dehydration, failure to thrive, prerenal AKI, hypokalemic arrhythmia
Persistent alkalosis increases perioperative apnea risk; surgery can cause mucosal perforation or incomplete myotomy
Brief postoperative emesis can occur; persistent worsening vomiting warrants reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: No reliable primary prevention; avoid unnecessary neonatal macrolides, without withholding necessary treatment
Early recognition of progressive vomiting prevents severe electrolyte depletion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Physiologic reflux: effortless small spit-ups, normal growth
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting, acute illness; urgent upper GI evaluation/surgery
Milk-protein allergy: bloody stools, eczema, feeding intolerance rather than fixed outlet obstruction

hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric surgery teaching.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.scope: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, autoimmune associations, levothyroxine dosing, TSH monitoring
hypothyroidism.core: Insufficient thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and delayed reflex relaxation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hashimoto autoimmunity, family history of autoimmune disease; thyroid surgery/radioiodine, iodine deficiency/excess
Lithium, amiodarone, postpartum thyroiditis; pituitary surgery/radiation or mass
Congenital primary → **thyroid dysgenesis** most common, not lymphocytic thyroiditis

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight gain, bradycardia, hoarseness, heavy menses, hyperlipidemia; hyponatremia in severe disease
★ **Hypothermia, altered mentation, hypoventilation, hypotension** → myxedema coma
Autoimmune clustering: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, celiac disease
Infant: macroglossia, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, large fontanelle → **TSH/free T4**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced hormone activity lowers thermogenesis and cardiac output; glycosaminoglycan deposition produces nonpitting edema
Hashimoto: lymphocytic infiltration; firm painless goiter, even if euthyroid; **anti-TPO/antithyroglobulin** antibodies

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and free T4** establish hormone deficiency and localize the level of dysfunction
Positive anti-TPO predicts progression from subclinical disease; ultrasound unnecessary without nodule/goiter concern
Recheck mild isolated TSH elevation after transient illness resolves; exclude medication interference

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Levothyroxine**; healthy young adult approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; older/CAD start 12.5–25 mcg/day
Fasting, apart from calcium/iron; TSH at 6–8 weeks; **persistently high → increase dose**, even if asymptomatic
Central disease: titrate using free T4; evaluate/replace cortisol before thyroid hormone
Subclinical, untreated: generally start at TSH ≥10; consider symptoms, antibodies, pregnancy at lower values
★ Myxedema: **IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone**, airway support, cautious fluids/passive warming; treat trigger

rows.label: Complications
items: Dyslipidemia, infertility, pericardial effusion, neuropathy; severe disease → respiratory failure
Excess replacement → AF, angina, bone loss; rapid correction in CAD can precipitate ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Pregnancy: early **TSH monitoring**, usually increase existing replacement promptly; use pregnancy-specific targets
Monitor stable replacement at least annually; address adherence/absorption before escalating doses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Depression, dementia, psychosis: normal TSH; hypothyroidism itself can cause reversible cognitive or psychiatric symptoms
Euthyroid sick syndrome: acute systemic illness, often low T3; avoid routine hormone replacement

hypothyroidism.evidence: Not checked online; established thyroid replacement and endocrine emergency teaching.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage (most common) or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids/vitamin A supplements

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late, compensatory; treat ICP, not BP
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema
IIH: **impaired CSF resorption** at arachnoid granulations; ventricles normal/small, no obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings → **LP**: normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction
Recent shunt revision + fever + neutrophilic CSF → **shunt infection**, not community meningitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway/intubation first**, head elevation, IV **hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis; PSC particularly associated with UC
Erythema nodosum: tender nonulcerating nodules; **pyoderma gangrenosum**: rapid painful violaceous ulcer, purulent base
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention, colon >6 cm → **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → CT/MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Partial SBO, suspected stricture → enterography; older exam questions may expect **water-soluble small-bowel follow-through**
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Moderate/severe flare without obstruction or abscess → **prednisone** induces remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression
UC with colorectal cancer → **total proctocolectomy**, not segmental colectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas (enterovaginal → vaginal flatus), strictures, obstruction in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Terminal ileal Crohn → B12 deficiency, **bile salt malabsorption** → steatorrhea
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

table.title: Distribution and outpatient treatment
rows: RLQ mass, cobblestones, perianal disease, granulomas
Bloody diarrhea, tenesmus; friability, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps

intrauterine-fetal-demise.name: Intrauterine fetal demise
intrauterine-fetal-demise.scope: Ultrasound diagnosis (absent cardiac activity), delivery methods (induction of labor, dilation and evacuation), maternal complication (DIC from retained fetus), postmortem evaluation (autopsy, karyotype)
intrauterine-fetal-demise.core: Suspected fetal death from absent movement or heart tones requires ultrasound confirmation before delivery planning and etiologic evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Placental insufficiency/FGR, hypertension, diabetes, abruption, infection, congenital anomalies, alloimmunization
Prior stillbirth, smoking, obesity, advanced maternal age, post-term pregnancy; many cases remain unexplained

rows.label: Clues
items: Reduced/absent fetal movement; absent Doppler tones alone insufficient
Bleeding or pain suggests abruption; fever suggests infection; maternal symptoms may be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fetal hypoxia, hemorrhage, infection, or lethal anomaly terminates circulation
Prolonged retention can release tissue factor, producing consumptive coagulopathy; uncommon with timely management

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ultrasound: absent fetal cardiac activity**; ensure diagnostic certainty and offer confirmation
★ Evaluate **placenta/cord histology, fetal autopsy, and genetic testing**; microarray often preferred to karyotype
Obtain fetal/placental tissue or amniotic fluid for genetics; maternal blood tests cannot substitute
Maternal CBC, coagulation/fibrinogen if retention/bleeding; prompt fetomaternal hemorrhage testing before delivery
Target APS testing, syphilis and diabetes evaluation to context; routine inherited thrombophilia/TORCH panels low value

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Offer compassionate **induction or D&E**, guided by gestation, preference, expertise, and uterine scar
Second trimester: mifepristone then misoprostol; later gestation: cervical ripening/oxytocin with scar-specific precautions
★ **Cesarean rarely indicated solely for demise**; maternal safety determines route
Bleeding/infection/DIC → stabilize, expedite; trauma + free fluid → emergent **cesarean**; anti-D if Rh-negative unsensitized
Provide bereavement care, memory-making options, lactation counseling, and follow-up review of results

rows.label: Complications
items: DIC, infection, hemorrhage; profound grief, depression, post-traumatic stress

rows.label: Prevention
items: Optimize identified maternal disease, stop smoking; future pregnancy: growth assessment and tailored fetal surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Fetal sleep: temporarily reduced movement but cardiac activity present
Dating/technical error: ultrasound demonstrates living fetus despite absent handheld Doppler signal

intussusception.name: Intussusception
intussusception.scope: Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception, pathologic lead points (Meckel, polyp), target sign on ultrasound, air enema
intussusception.core: Bowel telescoping causes intermittent obstruction and ischemia, often in a previously healthy infant with episodic distress and deceptively well intervals.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually age 6–36 months; lymphoid hyperplasia after viral illness
Older child, recurrent episode or adult → pathologic lead point: Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Sudden recurrent **colicky pain with knees drawn up**, pallor and vomiting
Lethargy/pallor between spasms can mimic neurologic illness; bilious emesis or distention suggests progressing obstruction
Sausage-shaped RUQ mass, empty RLQ; currant-jelly stool is late and often absent
Shock, guarding, fever or peritonitis → compromised bowel/perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Proximal bowel and mesentery invaginate distally → venous congestion, edema and arterial ischemia
Ileocolic location most common in children; bleeding reflects injured mucosa

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound first** → target/doughnut on transverse view, pseudokidney longitudinally
Plain radiograph for obstruction/free air when severe findings; normal radiograph does not exclude
CT generally for adult cases or uncertain alternative diagnosis, not routine pediatric first test
Classic clinical triad uncommon; do not delay testing until bloody stools appear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV fluids**, analgesia; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Stable without peritonitis/perforation → **air or contrast enema**: diagnostic and therapeutic, surgical backup
Failed reduction, perforation, shock or peritonitis → urgent surgery; resect nonviable bowel
Persistent/recurrent disease or suspected lead point → surgical evaluation; adult cases usually require resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, shock; recurrence after successful reduction
Enema-associated perforation → immediate surgical management

rows.label: Prevention
items: No usual primary prevention for idiopathic disease; remove identified pathologic lead point
After reduction → observe recovery, resume intake when tolerated; counsel on recurrent episodic symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: diarrhea predominates, less discrete symptom-free intervals
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting in neonate, urgent surgical evaluation
Meckel bleed or juvenile polyp: painless rectal bleeding, no colicky episodes

irritable-bowel-syndrome.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
irritable-bowel-syndrome.scope: Rome IV criteria, IBS subtypes (IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M), alarm features, low FODMAP diet, antispasmodics, fiber supplementation
irritable-bowel-syndrome.core: Recurrent abdominal pain linked to defecation and altered stool frequency/form, without alarm findings, supports a positive diagnosis of IBS.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Younger age, female sex, anxiety/depression, adverse life stress, previous enteric infection
Food-related symptom flares common; psychosocial associations do not make symptoms imaginary

rows.label: Clues
items: **Cramps relieved by defecation**, sometimes worsened; bloating, urgency, mucus, incomplete evacuation
★ **Bleeding, anemia, weight loss, fever, nocturnal diarrhea**, family cancer/IBD history → evaluate organic disease
New onset in older adults warrants careful assessment and age-based colorectal cancer screening

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Disordered gut–brain signaling, visceral/smooth-muscle hypersensitivity, altered motility and microbiome contribute
No destructive mucosal inflammation; subtype follows predominant abnormal stool consistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Rome IV**: pain ≥1 day/week over prior 3 months, symptom onset ≥6 months earlier
At least two: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form
CBC; diarrhea phenotype → celiac serology and fecal calprotectin/lactoferrin ± CRP when no alarms
★ **No routine colonoscopy** in younger patients meeting criteria without warning signs or screening indication
Review medications, lactose intolerance, infectious exposures; stool pathogen tests only when suggested by history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Soluble fiber/psyllium**, regular meals, exercise; limited low-FODMAP trial with structured reintroduction
Gut-directed CBT/hypnotherapy; peppermint oil may help pain; TCA useful for persistent pain, especially diarrhea
Dicyclomine: selected episodic cramping; anticholinergic harms, weak global-symptom evidence; avoid routine use

rows.label: Complications
items: Quality-of-life impairment, restrictive diets, anxiety; no increased colorectal cancer risk from IBS itself
Eluxadoline: pancreatitis risk, contraindicated without gallbladder; avoid escalating opioids

rows.label: Prevention
items: Identify dietary/stress triggers, maintain activity; avoid prolonged unnecessary elimination diets
Reassess new alarm findings rather than attributing every symptom to established IBS

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBD: objective inflammation/bleeding; celiac: positive serology, malabsorption
Microscopic colitis: watery nocturnal diarrhea, normal-looking colon, diagnostic biopsies

table.title: Stool subtype and targeted treatment
rows: PEG for constipation; linaclotide/lubiprostone for global symptoms
Loperamide for diarrhea; rifaximin for global symptoms

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness means retinal embolism from the ipsilateral carotid.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Hypertension: greatest modifiable risk factor**; smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: **Broca** nonfluent, poor repetition, intact comprehension; **Wernicke** fluent paraphasias, poor comprehension, no insight
Crossed: **Weber** ipsilateral CN III, contralateral hemiparesis (midbrain); lateral pons: ipsilateral full-face palsy, deafness
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction, often embolic; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF/cardioembolic → oral anticoagulation, timing by infarct/bleeding risk; noncardioembolic → antiplatelet only
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit
Long-term antiplatelet (aspirin allergy → clopidogrel); undertreated hypertension → **intensify antihypertensives**; high-intensity statin

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

table.title: Vascular localization
rows: Occipital: contralateral homonymous hemianopia; macular sparing
Diplopia, vertigo, dysarthria, ataxia, crossed/bilateral signs, coma
Vertigo; ipsilateral Horner/face/ataxia/palate; contralateral body pain-temperature

lactose-intolerance.name: Lactose intolerance
lactose-intolerance.scope: Primary lactase deficiency, secondary lactase deficiency, hydrogen breath test, stool reducing substances, dietary restriction, lactase replacement
lactose-intolerance.core: Bloating, flatulence and watery diarrhea after lactose ingestion reflect carbohydrate malabsorption rather than milk-protein allergy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary lactase nonpersistence increases after childhood and varies by ancestry
Secondary brush-border injury: viral gastroenteritis, celiac disease, Crohn disease, giardiasis
Congenital lactase deficiency rare; preterm infants can have transient developmental enzyme deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Dose-related cramps and gas within hours after milk/ice cream; symptoms improve without lactose
Stools lack blood; isolated intolerance does not cause fever or systemic inflammation
Infants with secondary malabsorption may develop acidic diarrhea and perianal irritation
Weight loss, anemia, nocturnal diarrhea or persistent symptoms despite restriction suggest another disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Low intestinal lactase prevents lactose cleavage into absorbable glucose/galactose
Unabsorbed sugar retains luminal water; bacterial fermentation produces hydrogen and organic acids

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms → **lactose elimination and rechallenge**; history often sufficient
★ Uncertain diagnosis → **hydrogen breath test** after lactose; rising hydrogen with symptoms supports intolerance
Stool reducing substances and low pH can support infant carbohydrate malabsorption; limited specificity
Persistent/refractory symptoms → targeted evaluation for celiac disease, giardiasis or other mucosal injury
Distinguish lactose malabsorption on testing from clinically symptomatic intolerance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reduce lactose to tolerated amount**; complete lifelong dairy exclusion usually unnecessary
Lactase enzyme with lactose-containing meals or lactose-free dairy; divided portions with food improve tolerance
Yogurt with live cultures and aged hard cheese often tolerated better than milk
★ Maintain **calcium and vitamin D** through tolerated foods, fortified alternatives or supplements
Treat secondary cause; retry lactose after mucosal recovery rather than assuming permanent deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Unnecessary dairy restriction → low calcium intake and impaired bone health
Severe infant diarrhea can cause dehydration; uncomplicated adult intolerance does not damage intestinal mucosa

rows.label: Prevention
items: Identify personal threshold; review lactose in foods and maintain nutritionally complete substitutes
Temporary reduced intake after gastroenteritis may help selected persistent cases

rows.label: Mimics
items: Milk-protein allergy: eczema, wheeze, urticaria or bloody infant stools
Celiac disease: nutrient deficiencies and positive tTG-IgA
IBS: broader food/stress triggers, no reproducible lactose-specific pattern

lead-poisoning.name: Lead poisoning
lead-poisoning.scope: Occupational exposure, moonshine, pediatric lead toxicity, basophilic stippling, motor neuropathy (wrist drop, foot drop), encephalopathy, dimercaprol, succimer chelation
lead-poisoning.core: Exposure-related abdominal colic, anemia, and neurologic dysfunction; children may have developmental injury despite appearing well.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pre-1978 paint dust, contaminated water/soil, imported remedies or pottery; pica increases exposure
Battery manufacture/recycling, construction, firing ranges, moonshine; occupational dust carried home

rows.label: Clues
items: Children: irritability, constipation, learning/behavior problems; severe cases → seizures, encephalopathy
Adults: **motor-predominant neuropathy** with wrist/foot drop, hypertension, renal dysfunction, saturnine gout
Microcytic or normocytic anemia; basophilic stippling supportive but neither sensitive nor specific

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase → impaired heme synthesis
Calcium mimicry disrupts neuronal signaling; deposition in bone creates long-lived stores

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous blood lead level** confirms elevated capillary screening; do not rely on hair testing
★ Pediatric reference **3.5 µg/dL** triggers exposure intervention; no safe childhood level
CBC, iron studies, renal function; abdominal radiograph for suspected ingested lead objects/paint chips
Developmental assessment; assess siblings and household exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove exposure; involve environmental health/toxicology; correct iron deficiency and support calcium intake
Child **45–69 µg/dL**, no encephalopathy → oral succimer with expert supervision
★ Encephalopathy or ≥70 µg/dL → admit; **dimercaprol followed by calcium disodium EDTA**
Radiopaque lead in bowel → polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation when safe
Adults: neuropathy, colic, high level → **calcium disodium EDTA** or succimer; pediatric thresholds don't apply

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent cognitive deficits despite chelation; CKD, infertility, pregnancy complications
EDTA can injure kidneys; disodium EDTA causes fatal hypocalcemia—use calcium disodium formulation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Certified lead abatement, wet cleaning, occupational protective measures; avoid contaminated products
Medicaid childhood screening at 12 and 24 months; otherwise risk/local screening program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron deficiency: low ferritin; can coexist and increase lead absorption
AIP: marked urinary PBG elevation, no characteristic lead anemia

lifestyle-counseling.name: Lifestyle counseling
lifestyle-counseling.scope: Physical activity, healthy diet, weight loss, prediabetes prevention
lifestyle-counseling.core: Collaborative, specific behavior goals improve cardiovascular risk, functional health, weight, and progression from prediabetes to diabetes.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ Adults with **overweight/obesity, prediabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia**, or low activity
Assess food access, mobility, culture, sleep, stress, tobacco, alcohol, and readiness to change
Obesity → ↑postmenopausal **breast cancer**, back pain; weight loss + exercise lower risk

rows.label: Schedule
items: ★ Aim **150 minutes/week moderate aerobic activity** plus strength training ≥2 days/week
Start below target if sedentary; progressive increases and reduced sitting still provide benefit
Children/adolescents: about 60 minutes daily activity; tailor to development and ability

rows.label: Special groups
items: Prediabetes: structured Diabetes Prevention Program; target 5–7% weight loss
Older adults: add balance/functional training; preserve protein intake and resistance exercise
Pregnancy: adapted activity and nutrition; avoid intentional weight-loss dieting

rows.label: Choice
items: ★ **Mediterranean/DASH pattern**: vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, unsaturated fats
Reduce sugary drinks/refined foods; calorie deficit for weight loss; individualize macronutrients
Motivational interviewing, SMART goals, follow-up; multicomponent obesity care; relapse → revise goals

rows.label: Contraindications
items: Unstable angina, decompensated HF, acute illness → stabilize before vigorous exercise
Insulin/sulfonylureas → plan glucose monitoring and hypoglycemia prevention around activity

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Metformin prevention for selected **high-risk prediabetes**; lifestyle support remains necessary
Aerobic exercise ↑HDL, fitness even at **normal BMI**; avoid judging success solely by scale
Back pain prevention: **exercise**, not activity restriction; older exam questions may expect weight loss

lifestyle-counseling.evidence: Prediabetes targets checked 2026-10-30: [CDC prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes-prevention/lifestyle-change-program/index.html); other counseling: established teaching.

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, no heavy lifting until pain resolves, heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical therapy if pain persists despite NSAIDs; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise
Vascular claudication: calf pain, bicycling too; standing still relieves; weak pulses alone don't exclude stenosis

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates
Shopping-cart sign; pulses usually preserved; MRI confirms

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.scope: Non-small cell, small cell, paraneoplastic syndromes, Pancoast, screening
lung-cancer.core: Persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, or a suspicious lung lesion requires tissue diagnosis and staging before treatment selection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, radon, asbestos, occupational carcinogens, prior thoracic radiation; adenocarcinoma also occurs in never-smokers
Leading cause of cancer death in men and women; smoking is the predominant risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Recurrent focal pneumonia, hoarseness, unexplained pleural effusion
★ **Pancoast tumor**: shoulder/ulnar-arm pain + ipsilateral Horner syndrome
SVC obstruction: facial swelling, neck-vein distention; cord compression or airway compromise requires urgent action
Painful long-bone periostitis ± clubbing/joint swelling → **hypertrophic osteoarthropathy**, a lung cancer complication

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bronchogenic malignant transformation → local invasion, lymphatic spread, hematogenous metastasis
Ectopic hormone production and immune cross-reactivity cause paraneoplastic syndromes
Central endobronchial tumor → bronchial obstruction → **post-obstructive pneumonia**, atelectasis, lobar collapse
Ectopic **ACTH** (polypeptide; cortisol excess secondary) → hyperpigmentation, hypertension, hypokalemic alkalosis, proximal weakness

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious finding → **contrast chest CT**; biopsy easiest site that establishes highest stage
Central lesion/nodes → bronchoscopy/EBUS; peripheral lesion → CT-guided biopsy; effusion → cytology
PET/CT for extracranial staging, brain MRI for selected stages/small-cell disease; pulmonary function before resection
Molecular profiling and PD-L1 guide advanced NSCLC treatment; suspicious nodes often require pathologic staging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early operable NSCLC → **surgical resection + nodal evaluation**; inoperable localized → stereotactic radiation
Locally advanced NSCLC → combined systemic treatment/radiation ± surgery in selected patients
Metastatic NSCLC → biomarker-directed agents or immunotherapy/chemotherapy
★ Small-cell → **platinum + etoposide**, stage-dependent radiation/immunotherapy; surgery rarely used
SVC syndrome from small-cell → urgent **chemotherapy** ± radiation; stent if severe; diuretics not definitive

rows.label: Complications
items: Brain/bone/adrenal/liver metastases, malignant effusion, thrombosis, respiratory failure
Radiation pneumonitis; checkpoint inhibitors → immune pneumonitis/endocrinopathies

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **annual low-dose CT**, age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, current smoking or quit <15 years
Stop after 15 quit-years or limited curative candidacy; **ACS omits quit-time restriction**
Smoking cessation and radon mitigation; chest radiographs do not substitute for screening CT

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB/fungal granuloma: microbiologic evidence; PET uptake not specific for cancer
Hamartoma: fat/popcorn calcification; pneumonia: clinical/radiographic response to antibiotics

lung-cancer.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2021](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening), [ACS 2023 guideline](https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.3322/caac.21811); treatment: established stage-based framework.

malaria.name: Malaria
malaria.scope: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax and ovale (hypnozoites), severe malaria, chemoprophylaxis, thick and thin blood smears
malaria.core: Fever after travel to an endemic region, with thrombocytopenia or hemolysis: exclude malaria urgently even after reported prophylaxis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Anopheles mosquito exposure; nonimmune travelers, pregnancy, young children, absent/incomplete chemoprophylaxis

rows.label: Clues
items: Rigors, sweats, headache, anemia, splenomegaly; fever need not follow textbook periodicity
★ **Severe: altered consciousness, seizures, shock, AKI, ARDS, acidosis, hypoglycemia, or parasitemia ≥5%**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Falciparum-infected erythrocytes adhere to endothelium → microvascular sequestration and organ injury
Vivax/ovale dormant hepatic **hypnozoites** → later relapses despite blood-stage clearance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Urgent **thick smear detects parasites; thin smear identifies species and quantifies parasitemia**
Negative initial smear + suspicion → repeat every 12–24 h, total 3 sets
Rapid antigen test supplements microscopy; CBC, glucose, creatinine, bilirubin, lactate assess organ injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe disease → **IV artesunate**, ICU support, then complete oral regimen; never delay for species identification
Falciparum/unknown → artemether-lumefantrine; **CDC 2026: 5 days**, formerly 3; initially hospitalize
Chloroquine-sensitive vivax/ovale → chloroquine; resistant acquisition → artemether-lumefantrine
★ Anti-relapse: **primaquine or tafenoquine only after quantitative G6PD testing**; avoid during pregnancy
Pregnant vivax/ovale → defer liver-stage treatment; suppressive chloroquine after acute treatment when susceptible

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral malaria, severe anemia, renal failure, death
Artesunate → delayed hemolysis; CBC weekly for 4 weeks

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **DEET, permethrin-treated clothing/nets**; destination-specific prophylaxis before, during, and after exposure
Pregnancy: chloroquine where sensitive; mefloquine for chloroquine-resistant, mefloquine-susceptible destinations

rows.label: Mimics
items: Babesiosis: tick exposure, Maltese-cross tetrads; no hepatic stage
Dengue: marked myalgias, leukopenia, capillary leak; no intraerythrocytic parasites
Typhoid: sustained fever, abdominal symptoms; blood cultures positive

table.title: Common prophylaxis
rows: Severe renal impairment; pregnancy generally avoided

measures-of-disease-frequency.name: Measures of disease frequency
measures-of-disease-frequency.scope: Incidence, prevalence, cumulative incidence, incidence rate, attack rate, case fatality rate, mortality rate
measures-of-disease-frequency.core: Disease frequency requires a numerator, eligible denominator, and time frame; new events, existing disease, and deaths answer different questions.

rows.label: Definition
items: Population at risk excludes people already affected or unable to develop the outcome
Person-time sums observation until disease, death, loss to follow-up, or study end

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration** in steady state; compatible time units
Longer survival increases existing disease burden even without more new diagnoses
Cumulative incidence is probability; incidence density has inverse-time units

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Variable follow-up/open cohort → **person-time denominator**; fixed cohort/interval → risk
Prevalence → service planning; attack rate → outbreak food/exposure investigation
Primary prevention → fewer new cases → monitor **incidence**, not prevalence

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Case fatality denominator: cases; mortality denominator: population**
Deaths attributed to disease ÷ all deaths = proportionate mortality, not mortality rate
Cross-sectional surveys cannot directly establish incidence or temporal causation

table.title: Independent examples
rows: Current cases ÷ population at one time
New outbreak cases ÷ exposed at-risk people

measures-of-disease-frequency.evidence: Established epidemiologic definitions; no guideline-dependent recommendation.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adults: **S. pneumoniae** most common; seeded by pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis, CSF leak, asplenia
Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; advanced HIV/transplant/chemotherapy → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: subacute, high opening pressure ± CN VI palsy, CSF antigen; TB studies if lymphocytic, low glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal contacts within 7 days of onset → **rifampin or ceftriaxone**; droplet isolation until 24 hours treated
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

microcytic-anemia.name: Microcytic anemia
microcytic-anemia.scope: Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia
microcytic-anemia.core: Low hemoglobin with MCV <80 fL: distinguish depleted iron, inflammatory iron sequestration, globin underproduction, and defective heme synthesis.

rows.label: Risk factors
