items: Menstrual/GI blood loss, pregnancy, low intake, malabsorption → iron depletion
Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy → inflammatory anemia
Inherited hemoglobin disorders; alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia → disordered heme production
Preterm birth → low stores, screen toddlers; infant microcytosis → **dietary history** for excess cow's milk

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea; severe anemia → tachycardia, angina, syncope
Pica, koilonychia, restless legs suggest iron deficiency
Markedly low MCV, preserved hemoglobin, high RBC count, **normal RDW** (Mentzer <13) suggest thalassemia trait

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin suppression, impaired absorption and iron release; cytokines blunt **erythropoietin**
Sideroblasts: mitochondrial iron accumulation in erythroblasts from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear → ferritin**, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation
★ Ferritin **<45 ng/mL in anemia** supports iron deficiency; normal result cannot exclude during inflammation
★ Adult men/postmenopausal women with iron deficiency → **EGD + colonoscopy**; consider celiac testing
Hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected beta-thalassemia; alpha trait may require genetic testing; exposure → blood lead
Microcytosis + afebrile pain crisis, at-risk ancestry → **smear** for sickled cells (sickle–β-thalassemia)

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Iron deficiency → **oral ferrous sulfate**; intolerance/malabsorption or rapid replacement need → IV iron
Treat bleeding source; continue iron about 3 months beyond hemoglobin normalization; reassess nonresponse
Inflammatory anemia → treat underlying disease; selected CKD → iron ± erythropoietin
Sideroblastic: remove trigger, pyridoxine if isoniazid-related; severe thalassemia → transfusion/chelation

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency: developmental effects in children, adverse pregnancy outcomes
Repeated transfusion → iron overload, cardiac/hepatic injury; oral iron → constipation, dark stool
Four-gene α-deletion → **Hb Barts** (γ4) → severe fetal anemia, hydrops fetalis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate dietary iron, pregnancy supplementation, lead-exposure reduction
★ **No empiric long-term iron for thalassemia trait** without documented deficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute blood loss: initially normocytic; hemoglobin may lag volume loss
Hemolysis: reticulocytosis, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin

microcytic-anemia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA iron deficiency evaluation 2020](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/); remaining hematology established teaching.

mononeuropathies.name: Mononeuropathies
mononeuropathies.scope: Ulnar nerve entrapment (cubital tunnel, Guyon canal, claw hand), radial nerve palsy (wrist drop, Saturday night palsy), peroneal/fibular nerve injury (foot drop), electromyography, splinting, surgical decompression
mononeuropathies.core: Weakness and sensory loss following one peripheral nerve suggest focal compression or injury; preserved muscles supplied proximally help localize the lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Compression, fractures, repetitive motion, tight casts, diabetes; intoxicated immobilization → Saturday night radial palsy
Prolonged elbow flexion, cycling/hypothenar pressure, leg crossing, rapid weight loss
Lithotomy/hip hyperflexion → **femoral** under inguinal ligament; stirrup at fibular head → foot drop
Antecubital hematoma after venipuncture → **median at elbow**; hook of hamate fracture → ulnar in Guyon canal

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Ulnar: **Froment sign**, advanced fourth/fifth-digit clawing; impaired grip and fine finger tasks
Rapid progression, severe pain, multiple noncontiguous nerves → consider vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex
Supraspinatus/infraspinatus atrophy, sensation intact, overhead athlete → **suprascapular** entrapment
Medial plantar laceration → medial toe hyperextension; superficial radial → dorsal web numbness, no wrist drop

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal compression first causes conduction block/demyelination; severe or sustained pressure causes axonal loss
Axonal regeneration is slow; duration and severity predict recovery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Map strength, reflexes, and sensation; compare muscles sharing a root but supplied by different nerves
Persistent/uncertain deficit → **EMG/nerve conduction studies**; denervation may take weeks to appear
Trauma → radiographs; suspected mass/structural entrapment → ultrasound or MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove compression; activity modification, **splinting**, occupational/physical rehabilitation
Ulnar at elbow → night extension splint; radial palsy → wrist-extension splint
Foot drop → ankle-foot orthosis and gait training; inspect cast/brace pressure points
★ Progressive deficit/refractory entrapment → **surgical decompression**; nerve laceration → urgent repair evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Muscle atrophy, fixed contractures, chronic neuropathic pain, falls
Delayed recognition of ongoing compression → irreversible motor deficit

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged elbow pressure, excessive flexion, leg crossing; pad vulnerable areas during surgery/immobility
Optimize diabetes control; ergonomic adjustment and frequent position changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: L5 radiculopathy: root-pattern pain; weakness also in tibialis posterior and gluteus medius
C8 radiculopathy: additional median-innervated muscle weakness, proximal symptoms
Stroke: sudden deficit with upper motor neuron signs or additional central findings

table.title: Localize common lesions
rows: Ulnar hand intrinsics; forearm spared; wrist Tinel
Palmar ulnar digits; dorsal hand spared
Finger extension; wrist extension partly preserved

mononeuropathies.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

mood-stabilizers.name: Mood stabilizers
mood-stabilizers.scope: Lithium (therapeutic range, toxicity, hemodialysis, tremor, nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism), valproate (hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity), carbamazepine, lamotrigine (Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
mood-stabilizers.core: Match the drug to bipolar phase; narrow therapeutic windows, organ toxicity, interactions, and pregnancy risks drive selection.

rows.label: Use
items: Lithium: mania, maintenance, reduced suicide risk; valproate/carbamazepine: acute mania
Lamotrigine: bipolar depression prevention; ineffective for acute mania

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Lithium alters intracellular signaling; anticonvulsants reduce excitatory neurotransmission

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Lithium: **nephrogenic DI**, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism; fine tremor → **propranolol**
Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, weight gain
★ **Lamotrigine rash → stop immediately**; Stevens-Johnson risk increases with rapid titration

rows.label: Avoid
items: Valproate in pregnancy: neural tube defects, impaired neurodevelopment; carbamazepine also teratogenic
Lithium: severe renal impairment, dehydration; pregnancy counseling includes fetal cardiac risk

rows.label: Interactions
items: Thiazides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, NSAIDs increase lithium; volume depletion worsens toxicity
Carbamazepine: CYP induction, reduced contraceptive efficacy; valproate increases lamotrigine levels

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Lithium **12-hour trough**: maintenance usually 0.6–1.0; acute mania 0.8–1.2 mEq/L
Renal function, TSH, calcium; valproate CBC/LFTs; carbamazepine CBC, sodium, LFTs
Carbamazepine: HLA-B*1502 testing with relevant Asian ancestry; agranulocytosis, SIADH, severe rash

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Lithium toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion → stop lithium, IV saline
**Hemodialysis**: seizures/coma, life-threatening arrhythmia, or renal impairment with lithium >4 mEq/L
Consider dialysis: >5 mEq/L, confusion, or clearance >36 hours to <1; monitor rebound

multiple-myeloma.name: Multiple myeloma
multiple-myeloma.scope: CRAB features (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lytic lesions), SPEP/UPEP M-spike, serum free light chains, bone marrow biopsy (>10% plasma cells), MGUS, smoldering myeloma
multiple-myeloma.core: A clonal plasma-cell malignancy causes monoclonal protein production and organ damage; modern biomarkers can establish treatment-requiring disease before symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, Black ancestry, male sex, preexisting MGUS; usually no identifiable preventable exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **CRAB**: hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, lytic bone lesions
Back/rib pain, pathologic fracture, recurrent bacterial infection, high total protein, rouleaux
Acute weakness/back pain → cord compression; proteinuria or restrictive cardiomyopathy → consider AL amyloid

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Marrow expansion suppresses blood formation; osteoclast activation without osteoblast response causes bone destruction
Light chains injure renal tubules; low polyclonal immunoglobulins → **encapsulated bacteria**, e.g., pneumococcus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **SPEP/immunofixation + free light chains**, urine studies; light-chain disease may lack serum spike
★ **Bone marrow biopsy** quantifies clonal plasma cells; whole-body low-dose CT/MRI assesses bone disease
Active disease: ≥10% clonal marrow cells/plasmacytoma plus attributable CRAB or myeloma-defining biomarker
SLiM: marrow ≥60%; involved/uninvolved FLC ratio ≥100 with involved FLC ≥100 mg/L
MRI >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm defines active disease; bone scan may miss lytic lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Bortezomib-based combination** ± daratumumab/lenalidomide/dexamethasone; selected patients → autologous transplant
Hypercalcemia → saline plus antiresorptive; AKI → hydration, avoid NSAIDs/contrast and rapidly reduce light chains
Cord compression → dexamethasone and urgent MRI/radiation or surgery; treat infections promptly
MGUS/smoldering disease generally monitored; high-risk smoldering disease merits specialist assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Cast nephropathy, vertebral collapse, hyperviscosity, AL amyloidosis; treatment-related neuropathy, infections and thrombosis
Urine dipstick detects albumin, misses light chains; negative dipstick does not exclude cast nephropathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccines, bisphosphonates; proteasome inhibitors → antiviral prophylaxis; immunomodulators → thromboprophylaxis by risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metastatic carcinoma: destructive lesions without clonal plasma-cell findings
Waldenström macroglobulinemia: IgM, hyperviscosity/lymphadenopathy, usually no lytic lesions

multiple-myeloma.evidence: Criteria checked 2026-10-30: [IMWG diagnostic criteria](https://www.myeloma.org/newly-diagnosed/multiple-myeloma-diagnostic-criteria); treatment: established generalist teaching.

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, **Northern European ancestry**, family history; EBV, smoking, low vitamin D

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular loss, poor color vision, afferent pupillary defect, often normal fundus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired ipsilateral adduction, contralateral abducting nystagmus; convergence intact
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse/optic neuritis → **high-dose IV methylprednisolone**, not low-dose prednisone; refractory → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

muscular-dystrophies.name: Muscular dystrophies
muscular-dystrophies.scope: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin frameshift, Gowers sign, dilated cardiomyopathy), Becker muscular dystrophy, myotonic dystrophy (CTG repeat, myotonia, cataracts, balding), genetic testing
muscular-dystrophies.core: Progressive inherited muscle weakness: childhood pelvic-girdle weakness suggests dystrophinopathy; delayed relaxation with multisystem disease suggests myotonic dystrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Duchenne/Becker: X-linked recessive; affected boys, maternal carrier relatives; de novo variants common
Myotonic dystrophy type 1: autosomal dominant with anticipation; severe congenital disease often maternally transmitted

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Gowers maneuver** and calf pseudohypertrophy indicate proximal weakness
Dystrophinopathy: waddling gait, delayed motor milestones; preserved sensation
Grip/percussion myotonia: delayed muscle relaxation, often improving with repeated movement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dystrophin deficiency destabilizes muscle membrane → myofiber necrosis and fat/fibrous replacement
Myotonic dystrophy: toxic expanded-repeat RNA disrupts splicing in multiple tissues

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK → genetic testing**; dystrophin deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing if needed
Myotonic phenotype → DMPK repeat-expansion testing; muscle biopsy rarely needed
ECG/echocardiography and pulmonary function at diagnosis and serially; assess swallowing and sleep ventilation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Duchenne: **prednisone or deflazacort**, stretching, mobility support; specialist genotype-directed options
Cardiomyopathy → ACE inhibitor/ARB, add beta-blocker; respiratory weakness → assisted cough/noninvasive ventilation
Disabling myotonia → mexiletine after cardiac evaluation; high-grade conduction block → pacemaker
Avoid succinylcholine; dystrophinopathy also carries rhabdomyolysis risk with volatile anesthetics

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, restrictive respiratory failure, aspiration, scoliosis, contractures
Steroid-associated osteoporosis and adrenal suppression; myotonic dystrophy → sudden cardiac death

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Carrier testing and genetic counseling**; screen female dystrophin carriers for cardiomyopathy
Vaccination, nutritional support, bone health monitoring, regular cardiac/respiratory surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: SMA: areflexia, fasciculations, relatively modest CK elevation
Inflammatory myopathy: acquired weakness, inflammation; no characteristic inheritance pattern

table.title: Distinguishing types
rows: Distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy

muscular-dystrophies.evidence: Not checked online; established phenotypes and supportive treatment; novel genotype-specific treatments omitted.

neural-tube-defects.name: Neural tube defects
neural-tube-defects.scope: Anencephaly, spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, Chiari II malformation, maternal serum AFP, amniotic acetylcholinesterase, lemon and banana signs, folic acid prevention
neural-tube-defects.core: Neural tube closure failure by approximately 4 weeks after conception produces cranial or spinal defects; prevention must begin before pregnancy recognition.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low folate, prior affected pregnancy, maternal diabetes/obesity, valproate/carbamazepine, early-pregnancy hyperthermia

rows.label: Clues
items: Midline lumbosacral sac, lower-limb weakness, absent reflexes, bladder dysfunction with neural involvement
★ **Lemon skull and banana cerebellum** on fetal ultrasound suggest open spina bifida/Chiari II
Occult lesions: hair tuft, atypical deep dimple, hemangioma; normal skin does not guarantee normal cord

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Failed neurulation leaves neural tissue unprotected; CSF leakage contributes to hindbrain herniation
Folate supports nucleotide synthesis during rapid embryonic cell division

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Maternal serum **AFP at 15–22 weeks**; elevation → verify dating/number, detailed ultrasound
Open defects elevate AFP; closed occulta may not; cfDNA does not screen neural tube defects
★ Uncertain imaging → amniotic fluid **AFP and acetylcholinesterase**; target anatomy scan at 18–22 weeks
Postnatal spinal ultrasound in young infant or MRI for suspected occult dysraphism/tethered cord

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open spinal lesion: **prone positioning, sterile saline dressing**, avoid pressure/contamination; neonatal neurosurgery
Early closure; assess hydrocephalus, renal function and bladder emptying; intermittent catheterization when neurogenic
Selected prenatal myelomeningocele repair can improve motor outcomes/reduce shunting, with maternal and prematurity risks
Anencephaly → counseling, pregnancy options, and palliative neonatal care; no curative treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Hydrocephalus (Chiari II obstructs CSF), meningitis, orthopedic deformities, neurogenic bowel/bladder, recurrent UTI, kidney injury
Tethered cord may cause progressive weakness or continence changes during growth
Osteopenic insensate legs: new swelling → **X-ray** for occult fracture

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Folic acid 400–800 µg/day** before conception through early pregnancy for average risk
Prior NTD pregnancy → **4 mg/day**, starting ≥1 month before conception through first 3 months
Optimize diabetes, review antiseizure drugs before pregnancy; avoid prolonged overheating

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sacrococcygeal teratoma: solid/cystic mass, not exposed neural placode
Abdominal wall defect: elevated AFP but bowel outside abdomen on ultrasound

table.title: Lesions
rows: Meninges/CSF herniate; cord remains within canal

neural-tube-defects.evidence: Folate checked 2026-10-30: [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/folic-acid/hcp/clinical-overview/), [USPSTF 2023](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/document/ClinicalSummaryFinal/folic-acid-for-the-prevention-of-neural-tube-defects-preventive-medication); remaining content established teaching.

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.name: Neuromuscular junction disorders
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.scope: Myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism, repetitive nerve stimulation, autoantibodies
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.core: Fluctuating or descending weakness with preserved sensation localizes to neuromuscular transmission; reflexes, pupils, and exercise response separate major causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: MG: autoimmune disease, thymoma; LEMS: smoking/small-cell lung carcinoma
Botulism: improperly canned foods, injection wounds, infant honey or environmental spores

rows.label: Clues
items: MG: diplopia, ptosis, nasal speech, chewing fatigue; worse late day or repeated activity
LEMS: proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation; transient strength/reflex improvement after exertion
Botulism: cranial palsies → symmetric descending paralysis, autonomic dysfunction; infant constipation and floppy weakness
★ **Bulbar weakness or declining ventilation** → impending respiratory failure even with normal oxygen saturation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: MG: postsynaptic receptor/MuSK autoimmunity; LEMS: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel autoimmunity
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → impaired acetylcholine release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AChR antibodies**, then MuSK if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG
MG → chest CT for thymoma; bedside ice-pack improvement supports ocular disease
LEMS → P/Q calcium-channel antibodies and chest CT for cancer
★ Suspected crisis → serial **forced vital capacity/negative inspiratory force**; not pulse oximetry alone
Botulism → serum/stool/toxin testing via public health; treatment before confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: MG → pyridostigmine, steroid-sparing immunosuppression; thymectomy for thymoma or selected generalized AChR-positive disease
★ Myasthenic crisis → **airway support + IVIG or plasma exchange**, treat precipitant
LEMS → amifampridine and treatment of malignancy; immunotherapy for persistent autoimmune disease
★ Botulism → **heptavalent antitoxin**; infants → human botulism immune globulin; ventilatory support
Wound botulism → debridement/antibiotics; avoid aminoglycosides and magnesium with impaired junctional transmission

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, respiratory arrest; MG immunosuppression → infection; steroids may initially worsen weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review MG-exacerbating drugs; safe food preservation; no honey before age 1 year
LEMS → ongoing cancer surveillance if initial evaluation negative

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: usually ascending weakness and areflexia, possible sensory symptoms
Brainstem stroke: abrupt focal signs; motor neuron disease: fasciculations/UMN signs

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.evidence: Botulism checked 2026-10-30: [CDC clinical guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7002a1.htm); MG/LEMS: established teaching.

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.name: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.scope: COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition mechanism, renal adverse effects (sodium retention, acute kidney injury), gastrointestinal toxicity, cardiovascular risks
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.core: NSAIDs reduce pain, inflammation, and fever through cyclooxygenase inhibition, with gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular tradeoffs.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Pain, dysmenorrhea, renal colic, gout; **lowest effective dose, shortest duration**
Topical diclofenac for localized joint pain reduces systemic exposure

rows.label: Mechanism
items: COX-1: gastric/platelet/renal effects; COX-2: inflammatory prostaglandins and endothelial prostacyclin
Most reversibly inhibit enzymes; aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ ↓Prostaglandin/prostacyclin → **afferent arteriolar constriction** → AKI, hyperkalemia, sodium retention, hypertension/HF worsening
★ Gastritis, **ulcer/bleeding**; platelet inhibition except with selective COX-2 agents
MI/stroke; interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy (chronic daily use, papillary necrosis); bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma

rows.label: Avoid
items: Active GI bleeding, severe CKD, decompensated HF, peri-CABG setting
Pregnancy ≥20 weeks generally avoid; later gestation → ductal closure and fetal renal injury
Aspirin in children with viral illness → Reye syndrome

rows.label: Interactions
items: ★ ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID → **high AKI risk**
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets → bleeding; NSAIDs can increase lithium and methotrexate exposure

rows.label: Monitor
items: BP, edema, creatinine, K; assess melena/anemia and prior ulcer history
High GI risk → consider PPI; reassess need rather than automatically continuing indefinitely
Rising creatinine or BP → stop NSAID, switch to **acetaminophen**

rows.label: Traps
items: Celecoxib reduces GI/platelet effects but retains renal and thrombotic risks
Prescribed low-dose aspirin for obstetric indications remains an exception to pregnancy NSAID restriction
Do not combine multiple NSAIDs for additional analgesia

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.evidence: Pregnancy safety checked 2026-10-30: [FDA NSAID warning](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-recommends-avoiding-use-nsaids-pregnancy-20-weeks-or-later-because-they-can-result-low-amniotic); other pharmacology: established teaching.

normal-pediatric-variants.name: Normal pediatric variants
normal-pediatric-variants.scope: Thymic sail sign on chest radiograph, physiologic genu varum and valgum, tibial torsion, infantile hemangioma
normal-pediatric-variants.core: Age-appropriate anatomy and growth can resemble disease; symmetry, normal function, and expected evolution support reassurance instead of unnecessary intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Normal skeletal alignment changes with development; familial rotational profiles are common
Infantile hemangiomas more frequent with prematurity, low birth weight and female sex

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Symmetric painless findings with normal growth/function** favor physiologic variation
Asymmetry, pain, progression, short stature or abnormal neurologic examination → pathologic evaluation
Hemangiomas appear in first weeks, proliferate rapidly during infancy, then gradually involute
Periocular, airway/beard-distribution, ulcerating or large segmental lesions are high-risk, not simple cosmetic variants

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Growth remodels lower-limb alignment/rotation; normal thymic tissue may silhouette against the lung
Hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor with proliferative and involution phases, distinct from vascular malformation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symmetric limb variant → **clinical examination**, growth review and rotational profile
Imaging for red flags, atypical age or suspected metabolic bone disease; not routine physiologic bowing
Typical hemangioma → clinical diagnosis; ≥5 cutaneous lesions → hepatic ultrasound
Large segmental facial/lumbosacral lesion → evaluate associated structural anomalies with specialist guidance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance and observation** for physiologic alignment, thymic appearance, toddler genital self-touching without abuse signs
Special shoes/braces do not correct internal tibial torsion; persistent severe functional deformity → orthopedics
★ High-risk hemangioma → **early referral, oral propranolol**; selected superficial lesions → topical timolol
Give propranolol with feeds, hold during poor intake/vomiting; monitor bradycardia and hypoglycemia

rows.label: Complications
items: Unnecessary imaging, bracing or surgery; hemangioma → ulceration, amblyopia, airway obstruction or residual skin change
Multiple hepatic hemangiomas → high-output heart failure or consumptive hypothyroidism

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blount disease: progressive asymmetric tibial bowing; rickets: widened wrists, abnormal mineralization
Mediastinal mass: mass effect/distortion rather than soft thymic contour

normal-pediatric-variants.evidence: Hemangioma guidance checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2019 guideline](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/143/1/e20183475/37268/Clinical-Practice-Guideline-for-the-Management-of); skeletal variants: established teaching.

table.title: Expected developmental patterns
rows: Varum to toddler; valgum peaks age 3–4
Yellow papules on erythematous base; trunk, well neonate
Resolves in days; reassure, no cultures
Bilateral nocturnal calf pain; normal exam, massage relieves
Blue hands, feet, perioral; pink mucosa, normal SpO2
Benign, first 24–48 hours; warmer if cold

nutritional-deficiencies.name: Nutritional deficiencies
nutritional-deficiencies.scope: Vegan diet nutrient risks, tea-and-toast diet, vitamin and mineral supplementation, clinical manifestations
nutritional-deficiencies.core: Restricted intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements produce characteristic mucocutaneous, neurologic, hematologic, and skeletal findings; identify the missing nutrient and its cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupplemented vegan diet: B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc risks
Tea-and-toast diet, alcohol misuse, food insecurity, restrictive eating, institutionalization
Bariatric surgery, pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, bowel disease → specific or fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor wound healing, bruising, oral changes, neuropathy, bone pain; mixed deficiencies commonly coexist
★ **Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia** in malnutrition → thiamine deficiency; complete triad often absent
Night blindness → vitamin A; bleeding with prolonged PT → vitamin K
Dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia → niacin; periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, dysgeusia → zinc (TPN, penicillamine)

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient cofactors impair energy metabolism, collagen formation, hematopoiesis, or mineralization
Low intake differs from malabsorption: replacement route and lasting supplementation must match the mechanism
Vitamin D deficiency → ↓calcium absorption → **secondary hyperparathyroidism**: normal calcium at bone's expense

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diet and supplement history**, weight trend, oral/skin/neurologic examination; assess GI disease
CBC/ferritin, B12 ± methylmalonic acid, 25-OH vitamin D chosen by findings; avoid indiscriminate panels
Albumin is altered by inflammation/fluid status; not a stand-alone nutrition diagnostic test
Severely undernourished → baseline phosphate, Mg, K before nutritional rehabilitation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke syndrome → **parenteral thiamine promptly**; do not await laboratory confirmation
B12 deficiency with neurologic signs/malabsorption → parenteral replacement; folate only after B12 assessment
Vitamin D/calcium for deficient intake or osteomalacia; iron replacement with evaluation for blood loss
Vitamin C for scurvy; oral balanced nutrition plus cause-directed supplementation and dietitian support
★ Severe malnutrition → **slow refeeding + thiamine**, close phosphate/K/Mg monitoring and replacement

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible B12 neurologic injury, fractures, anemia, infection susceptibility
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia, respiratory failure; excess vitamin A → hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vegans → **reliable B12 supplementation**; fortified foods, calcium/vitamin D and iodine adequacy
Diversified diet, food access support, lifelong bariatric follow-up; avoid megadose supplementation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Scurvy versus vasculitis: perifollicular hemorrhage/corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, restricted produce intake
Hypothyroidism: fatigue and macrocytosis with elevated TSH

nutritional-deficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established nutritional deficiency and refeeding principles.

obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.name: Obesity and bariatric surgery
obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.scope: Lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy (GLP-1 receptor agonists), indications for bariatric surgery, postoperative nutritional and surgical complications
obesity-and-bariatric-surgery.core: Chronic excess adiposity with metabolic complications; sustained treatment combines nutrition, activity, behavioral support, medications, and sometimes metabolic surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Calorie-dense diet, inactivity, sleep deprivation, genetic susceptibility, food insecurity
Glucocorticoids, antipsychotics, insulin; investigate endocrine causes when examination suggests them

rows.label: Clues
items: BMI ≥30 kg/m²; central adiposity predicts cardiometabolic risk
Screen for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, fatty liver, osteoarthritis, depression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Adipose inflammation and insulin resistance; appetite regulation favors weight regain after weight loss
Bypass and sleeve alter gut signaling and intake; bypass additionally decreases nutrient absorption

rows.label: Dx
items: Weight trajectory, medication review, eating-disorder assessment; A1c, lipids, liver enzymes
★ Postoperative **tachycardia**, fever, abdominal pain → investigate anastomotic leak urgently

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Structured calorie deficit, activity, behavioral follow-up; **5–10% weight loss** improves metabolic disease
Child: **cut liquid calories** first (juice, excess whole milk); cause is total calorie surplus
Medications: BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with comorbidity; semaglutide or tirzepatide plus lifestyle changes
★ Avoid GLP-1 agents with **MEN 2/medullary thyroid carcinoma** history; avoid weight-loss drugs during pregnancy
★ **Surgical referral** by eligibility below; assess nutritional, operative, psychosocial readiness and lifelong follow-up

rows.label: Complications
items: Early: leak, bleeding, VTE; later: stricture, rapid-weight-loss gallstones, internal hernia with intermittent pain
Roux-en-Y: dumping after sugary meals, marginal ulcers; iron, B12, calcium, vitamin D deficiencies
Persistent vomiting → thiamine deficiency; give thiamine promptly before carbohydrate loading

rows.label: Prevention
items: Lifelong supplements and nutritional surveillance after surgery; avoid NSAIDs and tobacco after bypass
Small meals, fewer simple sugars for dumping; delay conception during rapid postoperative weight loss

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cushing syndrome: violaceous striae, proximal weakness, easy bruising
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, bradycardia; usually modest weight gain

osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.scope: DEXA scan T-score criteria, screening guidelines, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, vertebral compression fractures, bisphosphonates
osteoporosis.core: Fragility fracture or markedly reduced bone density identifies skeletal weakness, often silent until hip or vertebral fracture.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Postmenopause, older age, White/Asian ancestry, BMI <20, parental fragility hip fracture, smoking, alcohol >2 drinks/day
Glucocorticoids, early or surgical menopause, hypogonadism, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, immobility, rheumatoid arthritis

rows.label: Clues
items: Height loss, kyphosis, acute back pain with **midline point tenderness** after trivial strain suggest vertebral compression
Neurologic deficits, fever, or nocturnal pain suggest alternative spinal pathology

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bone resorption exceeds formation; microarchitecture deteriorates despite normally mineralized remaining bone
Estrogen deficiency increases osteoclast activity; steroids suppress osteoblasts and reduce calcium balance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Hip/spine DXA**; use T-scores in postmenopausal women and men ≥50
★ Hip/vertebral low-trauma fracture establishes diagnosis regardless of DXA; acute vertebral pain → **spine x-ray** before DXA
CBC, calcium, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D; targeted secondary-cause testing
Younger adults: Z-score ≤−2 suggests below-age bone density; T-score alone insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Alendronate or zoledronic acid** for qualifying fracture, osteoporosis-range DXA, or high FRAX risk; raloxifene/estrogen contraindicated after VTE
Osteopenia: treat if 10-year hip risk ≥3% or major osteoporotic risk ≥20%
Oral bisphosphonate: fasting water, remain upright; avoid esophageal disease, hypocalcemia, severe kidney dysfunction
Very high risk → teriparatide/romosozumab then antiresorptive; stopping denosumab requires follow-on antiresorptive
Vertebral pain: analgesia, mobilization, short bracing; procedures reserved for selected refractory cases

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Hip fracture** → immobility, thromboembolism, excess mortality
Bisphosphonates: rare jaw osteonecrosis/atypical femur fracture; denosumab: hypocalcemia, rebound vertebral fractures

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen **women ≥65**, younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; evidence insufficient for routine male screening
**Smoking cessation**, less heavy alcohol outrank supplements; weight-bearing/resistance exercise, fall prevention, dietary calcium/vitamin D
Prednisone-equivalent ≥2.5 mg/day for >3 months → fracture-risk assessment; prevent with **alendronate**, not estrogen/raloxifene

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomalacia: defective mineralization, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase
Myeloma: anemia, renal injury, lytic lesions; metastatic fracture: destructive focal lesion

osteoporosis.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2025](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/osteoporosis-screening%20); treatment: established fracture-risk framework.

ovarian-cysts.name: Ovarian cysts
ovarian-cysts.scope: Follicular cyst, corpus luteum cyst, theca lutein cyst (hyperstimulation), mature cystic teratoma (dermoid), unilocular vs multilocular, surveillance intervals, cystectomy indications, cyst rupture
ovarian-cysts.core: Most reproductive-age ovarian cysts are benign; morphology, symptoms, menopausal status, and persistence determine observation versus surgery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Ovulatory cycles, early pregnancy; ovulation induction → **hyperstimulated ovaries**; very high hCG → bilateral enlargement
Postmenopausal adnexal masses carry higher malignancy risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Incidental mass, pelvic pressure, unilateral discomfort; sudden pain after intercourse/exertion suggests rupture
★ Sudden severe pain with vomiting → **torsion**; syncope/hypotension → major intraperitoneal bleeding

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Functional lesions arise during ovulation; dermoids contain differentiated germ-cell tissues

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pregnancy test first; **transvaginal ultrasound** characterizes wall, septations, solid elements, flow, free fluid
Simple unilocular: thin wall, anechoic, no solid vascular component; multiloculation warrants closer characterization
Papillary/solid vascular components, thick septa, ascites → malignancy evaluation; CA-125 nonspecific premenopausally
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion; urgent clinical concern overrides reassuring imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stable functional/hemorrhagic cyst → analgesia, recheck after menses; unresolved → repeat ultrasound in **6–12 weeks**
Asymptomatic simple cyst above 5–7 cm premenopause, 3–5 cm postmenopause → ultrasound around 6–12 months
★ Hemodynamic instability → IV fluids/blood and urgent laparoscopy; torsion → detorsion with ovarian preservation
Persistent/enlarging, symptomatic, large, suspicious mass → surgery/referral
OCPs do not hasten functional-cyst resolution; older exam questions may expect OCP + 6-week recheck

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemoperitoneum, ovarian infarction, reduced ovarian reserve after surgery

rows.label: Prevention
items: Ovulation suppression may reduce new functional cyst formation; counsel urgent reassessment for acute pain

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG with pregnancy outside uterus
Tubo-ovarian abscess: fever, cervical motion tenderness, inflammatory complex mass

table.title: Cyst identities
rows: Luteal/early pregnancy; tender mass, crenulated vascular wall, hemorrhage
Bilateral multicystic ovaries; regress as hCG falls
Young; complex echogenic mass; fat, teeth, calcification

ovarian-cysts.evidence: Simple-cyst thresholds checked 2026-10-30: [SRU 2019 consensus](https://pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/radiol.2019191354); acute management established teaching.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones (prior postprandial biliary colic), heavy alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease
Blunt abdominal trauma + epigastric mass/raised enzymes → contrast CT for pancreatic/duodenal injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue: ↓insulin, ↓glucagon, normal insulin sensitivity; lipase may normalize

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase or amylase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT: diagnostic doubt, high fever/marked leukocytosis (necrosis?), deterioration, no improvement by 48–72 hours; not routine early
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency
Recurrent, no gallstones/alcohol → EUS or MRCP for ductal anatomy; older exam questions may expect ERCP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, reassessment, IV opioid analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** by 48 hours if tolerated; else enteral; older exam questions may expect initial bowel rest
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Uncomplicated/sterile: no antibiotics; infected necrosis: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancrelipase, fat-soluble vitamins, pain control; islet-loss diabetes → **insulin**, not sulfonylureas

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; necrosis, hemorrhage; **splenic vein thrombosis** → isolated gastric varices, normal liver
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

panic-disorder.name: Panic disorder
panic-disorder.scope: Panic attack criteria, unexpected recurrent attacks, agoraphobia, acute abortive therapy, maintenance therapy, medical rule-outs
panic-disorder.core: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of fear of recurrence or maladaptive behavioral change establish panic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, family history, trauma, anxiety sensitivity
Caffeine, stimulants, cannabis, decongestants, hyperthyroidism, withdrawal can provoke paniclike symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt intense fear peaks within minutes; palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, paresthesias, derealization
Attack requires ≥4 characteristic symptoms; fear of dying/losing control common
★ **Syncope, exertional onset, hypoxemia, focal findings**, sustained arrhythmia → medical cause until evaluated
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 situations where escape/help seems difficult, persisting ≥6 months

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Threat-circuit overactivation and catastrophic interpretation of benign sensations amplify autonomic symptoms
Hyperventilation lowers CO₂ → lightheadedness, perioral/distal tingling; avoidance reinforces anticipatory fear
**Sodium lactate infusion** provokes attacks: heightened panic sensitivity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after medical/substance review**; unexpected episodes distinguish disorder from predictable triggers
Vital signs, examination, ECG for cardiopulmonary symptoms; glucose/TSH or toxicology guided by history
Chest pain risk → ACS/PE evaluation rather than automatic psychiatric attribution
Assess depression, suicidality, substance use; agoraphobia may be diagnosed separately

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ During attack → **calm reassurance, slow breathing**, reduce stimulation after excluding danger
Severe acute episode → short-term lorazepam when needed; avoid with sedatives or substance-use risk
★ Maintenance → **CBT with interoceptive exposure and/or SSRI**, such as sertraline
Start SSRI low, titrate slowly; benefit takes weeks; venlafaxine alternative
Continue effective treatment after remission, then gradual taper; benzodiazepines not preferred long-term

rows.label: Complications
items: Agoraphobic avoidance, impaired function, depression, self-medication with alcohol
Benzodiazepine dependence/withdrawal; alprazolam → **between-dose rebound anxiety**; SSRIs may initially increase anxiety

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reduce caffeine/stimulants**, regular sleep/exercise, practice exposure and relapse-prevention skills
Paper-bag rebreathing discouraged (hypoxemia risk); older exam questions may expect it if SpO₂ normal

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: persistent tremor, heat intolerance, low TSH
SVT: documented abrupt regular tachycardia, not solely subjective palpitations
Social anxiety: fear tied to scrutiny rather than unexpected attacks
Mitral valve prolapse: incidental click/murmur; doesn't explain recurrent attacks with fear of recurrence

panic-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR and anxiety treatment teaching.

parasomnias.name: Parasomnias
parasomnias.scope: REM sleep behavior disorder (polysomnography, clonazepam), sleep terrors, sleepwalking (somnambulism), nightmare disorder, isolated sleep paralysis, reassurance
parasomnias.core: Unusual behavior or experiences during sleep are classified by timing, recall, and whether REM muscle atonia is lost or persists.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sleep deprivation, stress, fever, alcohol, OSA precipitate NREM arousals
REM behavior disorder: older men, synucleinopathies, SSRIs; sleepwalking/terrors often childhood

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Dream enactment with injury** → ask bed partner about kicking, punching, falling from bed
Isolated sleep paralysis: conscious but briefly unable to move at sleep onset or awakening

rows.label: Pathophys
items: NREM disorders: incomplete arousal from deep sleep; REM behavior disorder: loss of normal skeletal atonia
Sleep paralysis: REM atonia persists into wakefulness

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected REM behavior disorder → **video polysomnography** demonstrating REM without atonia
Typical childhood NREM events: clinical; atypical stereotyped episodes → video EEG/PSG
Assess snoring, sleep schedule, drugs, trauma, daytime sleep attacks

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ REM behavior disorder: **immediate-release melatonin or clonazepam**; melatonin favored with falls/OSA concerns
Sleep terrors/walking: reassurance, adequate sleep, scheduled awakenings for predictable frequent events
Nightmares: imagery rehearsal; trauma-associated nightmares → assess PTSD
Isolated paralysis: reassurance, regular sleep; accompanying cataplexy → evaluate narcolepsy

rows.label: Complications
items: Injury to sleeper/partner; clonazepam can worsen sedation, balance, sleep-disordered breathing
REM behavior disorder may precede Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, or multiple system atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safe bedroom**: remove weapons, pad furniture, secure windows; separate sleeping if violent
Avoid sleep deprivation/alcohol; treat OSA; review triggering antidepressants

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nocturnal seizures: brief stereotyped clusters, possible postictal findings
OSA: gasping arousals tied to obstructive respiratory events

table.title: Timing and recall
rows: Awake, oriented, detailed frightening dream recall

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent, traumatic, malignant, or recurrent effusion → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure
Early post-cardiac-surgery tamponade → **urgent mediastinal re-exploration**

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

perioperative-care.name: Perioperative care
perioperative-care.scope: Preoperative cardiac risk, pulmonary evaluation, surgical antibiotic prophylaxis, medication management, pain control
perioperative-care.core: Optimize active disease, estimate procedural and patient risk, and order testing only when the result could change perioperative management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **MI within 60 days**, decompensated HF → highest perioperative cardiac risk; older exam questions may expect MI within 6 months
Emergency, vascular or intrathoracic surgery; ischemic heart disease, heart failure, CKD, diabetes
Smoking, COPD, OSA, frailty, malnutrition and prior anesthesia complications

rows.label: Clues
items: Chest pain, new dyspnea, syncope or decompensated fluid overload require targeted evaluation
Poor functional capacity: inability to climb stairs or perform activities around 4 METs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Surgical stress raises myocardial oxygen demand; anesthesia can lower perfusion pressure
Sedation, pain and recumbency reduce ventilation and promote atelectasis and venous stasis
Surgical stress, pain, opioids → nonosmotic **ADH** release → transient oliguria with normal renal function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RCRI/NSQIP** plus functional assessment; no routine stress test for low-risk surgery
Elevated risk, poor/unknown capacity → stress test if management changes; cannot exercise → **pharmacologic stress imaging**
ECG for cardiovascular symptoms; echo for new/worsening HF or suspected significant valve disease
No routine chest radiograph/spirometry without respiratory findings; assess airway and OSA history
Lung resection: **predicted postoperative FEV1** best predictor of complications; predicted postoperative FEV1 <30–40% → high risk, exercise testing before deciding

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Active ACS, decompensated HF or unstable arrhythmia → defer elective surgery and stabilize
★ Continue chronic **beta blockers/statins**; do not start beta blockade on surgery day
Hold **SGLT2 inhibitors 3–4 days**; individualize GLP-1 drugs by aspiration risk; continue reduced basal insulin
★ **Cefazolin within 60 minutes** before incision; MRSA or severe beta-lactam allergy → vancomycin within 120 minutes
Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen, regional block, selective NSAID; add opioid by severity, respiratory monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial injury, AKI, delirium, pneumonia, VTE and surgical-site infection
Opioids aggravate OSA; excessive fluids can worsen pulmonary edema
New postoperative dyspnea, ↓basal breath sounds → chest radiograph first, before PE imaging or heparin

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, lung expansion exercises, early mobilization, mechanical/pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis
Anticoagulation interruption individualized; bridging reserved for highest thrombotic risk
Chronic steroid exposure with adrenal suppression → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage
Usable gut → **enteral feeding**, including distal jejunostomy, over TPN

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anxiety-related dyspnea: normal cardiopulmonary evaluation
Stable chronic disease: baseline symptoms alone do not mandate cancellation

table.title: Postoperative pain
rows: Severe pain after major abdominal surgery

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings
Abrupt onset + AF, even with prior claudication → **embolus**, not in situ thrombosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle
Subclavian stenosis proximal to vertebral origin → arm exercise reverses ipsilateral vertebral flow; brachiocephalic lesion: right arm + carotid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; acute ischemia: bedside Doppler, **arteriography with runoff**
Subclavian steal → **compare BP in both arms** (gap >15 mm Hg); confirm with duplex or **MR angiography**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia with distal target → **surgical bypass** before amputation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin, vascular consultation** without awaiting imaging; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible or nonfunctional limb (nonambulatory, contractures) → primary amputation
Popliteal aneurysm: pulsatile popliteal mass, distal emboli; large → **tibial nerve compression** (posterior knee/calf pain)

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings
Thoracic outlet syndrome: symptoms on arm abduction, no posterior-circulation ischemia

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals
Calf claudication; normal femoral, weak pedal pulses
Arm-exercise dizziness/syncope or claudication; weak ipsilateral pulse

peroxisomal-disorders.name: Peroxisomal disorders
peroxisomal-disorders.scope: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, adrenomyeloneuropathy, Zellweger syndrome, Refsum disease, very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA), phytanic acid, peroxisomal biogenesis
peroxisomal-disorders.core: Impaired peroxisomal lipid metabolism causes combinations of leukodystrophy, adrenal failure, neuropathy, retinopathy, or severe neonatal multisystem disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy: ABCD1 variants; males typically severe, female carriers can develop myelopathy
Zellweger spectrum and adult Refsum: usually autosomal recessive

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Boy with **behavioral/school decline, vision loss, spasticity ± adrenal insufficiency** → cerebral ALD
Adult spastic paraparesis, bladder/sexual dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy ± adrenal insufficiency → adrenomyeloneuropathy
Neonate with hypotonia, seizures, dysmorphism, liver disease → Zellweger spectrum
Retinitis pigmentosa, anosmia, ichthyosis, hearing loss and ataxic neuropathy → adult Refsum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ABCD1 dysfunction → impaired peroxisomal VLCFA transport/oxidation; Zellweger: defective peroxisome biogenesis
Refsum: impaired α-oxidation of branched-chain phytanic acid; differs from VLCFA β-oxidation defects

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Plasma VLCFA + molecular testing** for suspected ALD/Zellweger; assess adrenal function
Refsum phenotype → **plasma phytanic acid**, then molecular confirmation; VLCFA may be normal
Brain MRI: parieto-occipital white matter injury; AM cortisol/ACTH and stimulation testing identify adrenal deficiency
Normal VLCFA in a female does not exclude ABCD1 variant; use genetic testing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ ALD adrenal failure → **hydrocortisone**, add fludrocortisone if mineralocorticoid deficient; stress dosing education
Early active cerebral ALD → urgent specialist hematopoietic stem-cell transplant evaluation before advanced deficits
Adrenomyeloneuropathy: treat spasticity/bladder symptoms, rehabilitation; transplant cannot reliably reverse myelopathy
Zellweger: nutritional, seizure, hepatic and respiratory support
★ Refsum: **restrict dietary phytanic acid**, avoid fasting/rapid weight loss; severe arrhythmia/weakness → apheresis

rows.label: Complications
items: Adrenal crisis, progressive cognitive/motor loss; Refsum arrhythmia and blindness
Severe Zellweger: feeding failure, liver dysfunction, early mortality

rows.label: Prevention
items: Cascade testing and genetic counseling; ALD family/newborn identification enables serial MRI and adrenal surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Addison disease: adrenal failure without characteristic leukodystrophy
Metachromatic leukodystrophy: lysosomal enzyme defect; no primary adrenal failure

peroxisomal-disorders.evidence: Refsum management checked 2026-10-30: [GeneReviews](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1353/); established ALD/Zellweger teaching.

personality-disorders.name: Personality disorders
personality-disorders.scope: Cluster A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), Cluster B (borderline, antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic), Cluster C (avoidant, dependent, OCPD), dialectical behavior therapy
personality-disorders.core: Enduring, inflexible patterns of cognition, affect, relationships, or impulse control cause impairment across settings beginning by adolescence or early adulthood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperament, genetic susceptibility, early adversity and disrupted attachment; avoid attributing diagnosis to trauma alone
Traits must exceed cultural expectations; diagnose cautiously during acute illness or developmental transitions

rows.label: Clues
items: Cluster A: paranoid—distrust; schizoid—detachment; schizotypal—magical thinking, odd speech/perceptions, social discomfort
Cluster B: antisocial—violations of rights; histrionic—attention seeking; narcissistic—grandiosity/entitlement
Cluster C: avoidant—fears rejection/embarrassment, avoids new activities; dependent—clinging; OCPD—rigid perfectionism, control
★ Borderline: **splitting, unstable identity/relationships, self-harm**, abandonment fear, chronic emptiness, impulsivity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maladaptive trait patterns impair emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning; no diagnostic biomarker
Impulsive aggression, violent suicide → **low CSF 5-HIAA** (serotonin metabolite)

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Longitudinal clinical assessment** across contexts; obtain collateral with consent
Exclude mood episodes, psychotic illness, substances, neurodevelopmental disorders and acquired brain disease
★ Antisocial diagnosis requires **age ≥18 plus conduct disorder before 15**
Borderline may cause brief stress-related paranoia/dissociation; sustained psychosis requires broader evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Borderline → **dialectical behavior therapy**; structured psychotherapy and consistent team boundaries
Trait-matched psychotherapy, e.g., avoidant → **CBT**, assertiveness training; clear expectations, empathic, nonpunitive tone
No medication treats personality disorder globally; target comorbid depression/anxiety or limited severe symptoms
Self-harm threats → assess intent, plan, access and safety; imminent risk → emergency psychiatric care
Avoid staff splitting through shared care plans; avoid reflexive long-term benzodiazepines in impulsive patients

rows.label: Complications
items: Self-injury/suicide, substance misuse, impaired work/relationships; antisocial traits → legal or violence consequences
Stigma and inconsistent treatment worsen engagement; therapeutic ruptures require careful repair

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autism: early developmental social-communication differences and restricted interests
Delusional disorder: fixed delusion rather than generalized suspicious personality style

personality-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

table.title: Common diagnostic confusions
rows: Reactive hours-long shifts vs sustained mood episodes
Odd beliefs vs persistent frank psychosis

pharyngitis.name: Pharyngitis
pharyngitis.scope: Centor score, Group A Streptococcus, rapid antigen detection, throat culture, viral pharyngitis, penicillin, peritonsillar abscess
pharyngitis.core: Most sore throats are viral; identify patients needing group A streptococcal testing and recognize deep-space infection or airway danger.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: School-age children, close contacts, crowded settings, winter/spring; GAS uncommon below age 3
Smoking, immunosuppression, incomplete vaccination broaden infectious differential

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctivitis, oral ulcers** favor viral cause; avoid unnecessary GAS testing
Centor: fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough; 1 point each
McIsaac modifies by age; score 0–1 → no test, no antibiotic; scoring never proves bacterial infection
★ **Trismus, muffled voice, unilateral bulge, uvular deviation** → peritonsillar abscess

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GAS pharyngeal infection can trigger immune-mediated rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis
Tonsillitis → peritonsillar pus: **GAS** commonest, often mixed anaerobes; deeper spread threatens airway, vessels

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No clear viral syndrome and elevated clinical score → **rapid antigen test or NAAT**
Negative rapid antigen in symptomatic child ≥3 → throat culture; adults usually need no backup
Positive test with compatible illness → treat; asymptomatic carriage generally needs no eradication
Abscess usually clinical; ultrasound/contrast neck CT if uncertain or deep-space extension suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Confirmed GAS → **penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days**; IM benzathine penicillin if adherence uncertain
Penicillin allergy: cephalexin if nonimmediate; azithromycin/clindamycin if immediate, accounting for local resistance
Viral illness → fluids, warm saline gargle, acetaminophen/ibuprofen; no antibiotics
★ Peritonsillar abscess → **drainage + amoxicillin-clavulanate**; airway assessment, IV ampicillin-sulbactam if severe

rows.label: Complications
items: Rheumatic fever prevented by timely GAS antibiotics; poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis not reliably prevented
Retropharyngeal spread, airway obstruction; Fusobacterium → internal jugular thrombophlebitis/Lemierre syndrome

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene; remain home until afebrile and ≥12–24 hours after effective GAS antibiotics
Do not routinely test asymptomatic household contacts or obtain test-of-cure

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV: posterior nodes, splenomegaly, amoxicillin-associated rash
Epiglottitis: drooling, tripod posture, stridor; avoid provocative throat examination
Diphtheria: adherent gray membrane, incomplete vaccination

phobias.name: Phobias
phobias.scope: Specific phobia (flying, heights, blood-injection-injury), exposure therapy, situational benzodiazepines, social anxiety disorder (generalized vs performance-only), beta-blockers, agoraphobia
phobias.core: Persistent disproportionate fear leads to avoidance or endurance with intense distress, producing impairment despite recognition that danger is limited.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperamental inhibition, family anxiety, frightening experiences or learned fear; often childhood/adolescent onset

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Fear reliably provoked by trigger; duration **≥6 months**, excessive relative to actual/cultural danger
Anticipatory anxiety and avoidance limit school, work, medical care or travel
Blood-injection-injury subtype may produce vasovagal syncope rather than persistent tachycardia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conditioned threat response and avoidance prevent extinction; relief from escape reinforces fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical assessment** of trigger, feared consequence, avoidance and impairment
Agoraphobia: fear in ≥2 categories—transport, open/enclosed spaces, crowds/lines, outside home alone
Exclude substances, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia or pulmonary disease when bodily symptoms atypical
Symptoms only with feared trigger, normal exam → psychiatric evaluation, not pheochromocytoma/Holter workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Graded exposure-based CBT** first-line across phobic disorders
Blood-injection-injury: applied muscle tension during exposure reduces fainting
Generalized social anxiety: CBT or sertraline/escitalopram; venlafaxine alternative
★ Performance-only social anxiety → situational **propranolol**; asthma/bradycardia → short-acting benzodiazepine instead
Rare trigger (flight, MRI) → short-acting benzodiazepine (**↑GABA-A**); routine use risks dependence, impairs exposure

rows.label: Complications
items: Social/occupational restriction, depression, substance misuse; avoidance of necessary health care
Beta-blocker hypotension; benzodiazepine sedation, falls, impaired driving

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early treatment, repeated graduated practice and reduced avoidance help maintain gains
Avoid self-medication with alcohol; include relapse-prevention exposure plans

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks; fear of further attacks
OCD: intrusive obsessions and rituals drive avoidance
Avoidant personality: pervasive longstanding inadequacy/rejection sensitivity, often coexists with social anxiety

phobias.evidence: Social anxiety care checked 2026-10-30: [NIMH](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/social-anxiety-disorder-more-than-just-shyness); established exposure-based care.

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure
**Comprehensive, contextual care**: whole-person, longitudinal; tailored to culture, family, goals

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

table.title: Difficult conversations
rows: Pause; allow feelings; schedule prompt follow-up
Voice openly in patient's presence; no covert action
Capable patient hides news from family
Encourage support; respect privacy; never lie to family
Child asks prognosis, parents forbid disclosure
Explore understanding; encourage talking with parents; never lie
Negotiate adherence contract; punitive control backfires
Fluent bilingual staff acceptable; never a child

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

pleural-effusion.name: Pleural effusion
pleural-effusion.scope: Transudate vs exudate (Light criteria), parapneumonic effusion, empyema, malignant effusion
pleural-effusion.core: Fluid in the pleural space causes dyspnea, dullness, and reduced breath sounds; classify by mechanism and identify infection requiring drainage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome; pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, TB
Recent thoracic surgery, pancreatitis, esophageal rupture, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Pleuritic pain, reduced fremitus; large effusion shifts mediastinum away; unilateral + cancer history → malignant
Fever or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics suggests complicated parapneumonic fluid/empyema
Bloody fluid: malignancy (prior cancer, mediastinal mass), embolism, trauma; milky → chyle
Foul-smelling pus after aspiration → **anaerobic empyema**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transudate: altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressure; exudate: increased permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage
Heart-failure transudate: pleural protein <3 g/dL, low LDH and cell count; **glucose equals serum**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Chest radiograph → **ultrasound-guided thoracentesis** for new unexplained, unilateral, or atypical effusion
Classic bilateral heart-failure effusions → diuresis first; sample if fever, asymmetry, or treatment failure
★ **Exudate if any Light criterion** positive; compare paired pleural and serum measurements
Pleural pH, glucose, cell differential, Gram stain/culture; cytology if cancer suspected
Diuresis can create pseudoexudate; serum–pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL supports transudate

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat systemic cause; therapeutic thoracentesis for significant symptoms; avoid rapid excessive drainage
★ Pus, positive Gram stain/culture, **pH <7.20** or glucose <60 → empyema/complicated: chest tube, antibiotics
Loculated infected fluid → intrapleural tPA/DNase; persistent sepsis → VATS evaluation
★ Recurrent symptomatic malignancy → **indwelling pleural catheter** or pleurodesis; trapped lung favors catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, loculation, trapped lung, respiratory compromise
Thoracentesis → pneumothorax, bleeding, reexpansion pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Heart-failure control, prompt pneumonia treatment; ultrasound guidance reduces procedural injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atelectasis: mediastinal shift toward volume loss
Consolidation: increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds
Pneumothorax: hyperresonance rather than dullness

pleural-effusion.evidence: Not checked online; established pleural disease teaching.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.scope: Community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration, atypical pneumonia (Legionella, Mycoplasma)
pneumonia.core: Acute lower respiratory infection with a new infiltrate; severity, acquisition setting, and resistance risks determine disposition and empiric antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, COPD, age, immunosuppression
Dysphagia, absent gag/cough (stroke, dementia, Parkinson), impaired consciousness → aspiration
HAP ≥48 hours hospitalized; VAP ≥48 hours after intubation
Prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics → resistant pathogens

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, cough, sputum, focal crackles; older adults: confusion; children: lower-lobe disease may refer abdominal pain
★ Severe: **hypoxemia, hypotension, tachypnea**, multilobar disease; ventilation or pressors → ICU
Legionella: water exposure, diarrhea, hyponatremia; Mycoplasma: school-age/young adult, indolent dry cough, cold agglutinins
Immunocompromised, diffuse bilateral interstitial/alveolar infiltrates, exertional hypoxemia → **Pneumocystis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar inflammation/exudate → shunt and impaired oxygenation
Chemical aspiration pneumonitis: sterile gastric injury; severity tracks **volume and acidity**; rapid improvement possible

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CXR** first; CT if strong suspicion despite nondiagnostic radiograph
**CURB-65** 0–1 or low PSI → outpatient; severe CAP → blood/sputum cultures, Legionella antigen ± PCR
Low procalcitonin alone does not justify withholding initial antibiotics in radiographically confirmed bacterial CAP
Gram-positive lancet diplococci → **S pneumoniae**: commonest CAP; lobar consolidation, high fever, often post-viral URI
Small gram-negative coccobacilli, smoker/COPD → **H influenzae**

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen, fluids for hypoperfusion; drain empyema; narrow antibiotics to cultures
★ Aspiration pneumonia: usual CAP coverage; **add anaerobic coverage only for abscess/empyema**
Anaerobes: **ampicillin-sulbactam**; older exam questions may expect **clindamycin**, even without abscess
Stable nonsevere CAP: ATS 2025 permits 3–4 days; classic ≥5-day rule remains for severe disease
★ Severe noninfluenza CAP → consider **systemic corticosteroids**; nonsevere CAP → avoid routine steroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Parapneumonic effusion, empyema, bacteremia, respiratory failure, sepsis
S aureus: postinfluenza necrotizing pneumonia; child failing amoxicillin, dense consolidation/effusion
Aspiration (alcoholism, intubation) → **lung abscess**: dependent-segment cavity, air-fluid level, foul sputum
Antibiotic exposure → C difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, smoking cessation, swallowing evaluation
Aspiration/VAP prevention: head elevation 30–45°, oral care, early liberation from ventilation

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: thrombotic risk, pleuritic pain, no infectious source
HF: bilateral edema, elevated JVP, cardiac dysfunction

table.title: Empiric adult regimens
rows: Amoxicillin/clavulanate + azithromycin; doxycycline alternative; or levofloxacin
Antipseudomonal: cefepime, ceftazidime, or piperacillin/tazobactam; usually 7 days

pneumothorax.name: Pneumothorax
pneumothorax.scope: Spontaneous pneumothorax (primary, secondary), tension pneumothorax, needle decompression, chest tube thoracostomy
pneumothorax.core: Pleural air causes acute unilateral pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds; circulatory compromise indicates tension physiology requiring immediate decompression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: tall thin young adults, smoking, family history
Secondary: COPD, cystic fibrosis, PJP, interstitial lung disease; trauma/procedures or positive-pressure ventilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral hyperresonance, dyspnea, asymmetric chest expansion; severity depends on underlying reserve
